entry.title: Apache Arrow: A Source Tour of the Columnar Memory Format That Moves Your Data

link.title: Apache Arrow: A Source Tour of the Columnar Memory Format That Moves Your Data

entry.content:
Most machine learning stacks never admit how much time they spend converting data. NumPy wants one layout, pandas wants another, your trainer wants tensors, and the Parquet file on disk wants a third. Every conversion is a memcpy nobody budgeted for. Apache Arrow attacks exactly that problem: it is a specification for a columnar, in-memory representation — and a working implementation of it — so that a column stored on disk, shipped over a network socket, or handed to a GPU-adjacent library looks like the same bytes, laid out the same way, with the same null encoding. When the formats agree, “reading a file” can degenerate into pointing at memory you already have.

What makes Arrow worth a source tour is that the spec and the code are unusually close together. The C++ implementation in cpp/src/arrow/ is the reference behavior: buffers, types, validation, IPC framing, a compute kernel library, and a dataset scanner that hides files, partitions, and row groups behind one API. The Python package pyarrow is not a reimplementation — it is a thin Cython shell over the C++ objects, which is why a pyarrow.Table can be handed to pandas, Polars, DuckDB, or even the Hugging Face datasets library without anyone copying columns first. In this post we walk the repository from the Python surface down to the buffer pool, with two generated architecture diagrams to anchor the tour.

The two diagrams below were generated from the actual file tree of the repository. The overview shows the six moving parts a data engineer touches; the detail view zooms into the dataset layer, the CSV stack, and the memory infrastructure that make the zero-copy story real.

Apache Arrow end to end: pyarrow's Cython surface wraps the C++ core, whose arrays and record batches serialize through flatbuffer-based IPC, while the dataset layer drives format readers and compute kernels.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Python tabular surface. Everything starts in table.pxi, where the Cython classes live. The Table class, L4064 inherits from _Tabular, and constructors like Table.from_arrays, L4762 wrap C++ arrays behind a friendly signature. Relational sugar like Table.join, L5644 and Table.group_by, L5603 actually delegates to the compute layer rather than reinventing joins in Python.
  • Array wrapper. In array.pxi, the Array class, L1122 exposes the honest mechanics: Array.buffers, L1955 hands back the raw validity and data buffers, Array.to_numpy, L1782 decides whether a conversion is zero-copy or not, and Array.validate, L1920 checks structural invariants. If you have ever wondered what a “column” physically is, this is the file to read.
  • C++ Table core. On the C++ side, table.cc implements chunked composition. Table::CombineChunks, L599 consolidates fragmented columns, ConcatenateTables, L407 glues tables vertically, and TableBatchReader::ReadNext, L687 streams a Table back out as record batches — the unit that everything downstream actually consumes.
  • Record batches. record_batch.cc defines the column-aligned row group with a shared row count. RecordBatch::FromStructArray, L250 shows how a struct array of N fields becomes an N-column batch, and RecordBatch::SelectColumns, L423 is a pure metadata operation — no bytes move, because each column is just a pointer to a buffer.
  • The wire. Serialization lives in writer.cc. The RecordBatchSerializer class, L131 walks every buffer, writes its flatbuffer metadata, and pads body segments to 8-byte alignment; WriteRecordBatchStream, L874 sequences those messages into the stream format. This framing is what “Arrow IPC”, Feather V2, and a lot of network-facing data planes share.
  • The read side. In reader.cc, the ArrayLoader class, L173 replays that walk in reverse, attaching buffer views to freshly typed arrays, while StreamDecoderInternal, L1001 handles the incremental case for sockets and chunked streams. Read a file fast enough and you never materialize more than the output you asked for.
  • Dataset layer. dataset.cc turns “scan this directory” into an object model: Dataset::NewScan, L204 returns a builder, and fragments implement physical reads — see InMemoryFragment::ScanBatchesAsync, L106 for the trivial case. The async scanner in scanner.cc pushes fragments through a fan-out so batching stays ahead of the consumer; AsyncScanner::ToTable, L402 is the convenience exit point.
  • Format readers. Each file format plugs in as a FileFormat. The parquet one, file_parquet.cc, exposes ParquetFileFormat::ScanBatchesAsync, L592, which is where row-group pruning and column projection get applied. The CSV stack is pure Arrow: the streaming reader in csv/reader.cc (constructed via StreamingReader::Make, L1230) parses byte blocks, decodes columns, and emits batches incrementally.
  • Memory pools. Under everything sits memory_pool.cc, where SystemMemoryPool, L536 and the mimalloc-backed alternative at MimallocAllocator, L391 account for every allocation the library makes. Arrow tracks bytes deliberately: zero-copy only saves time if you can see where the copies are.

The detail view: kernels, fragments, and the buffer economy

The detail graph adds the array builders, IPC message envelope and dictionary memo, Feather compatibility, the function dispatch path, dataset discovery and writers, the CSV parser-to-decoder stack, and the memory pools underneath.

Two things deserve a closer look than the overview can give. First, the compute subsystem. Arrow’s kernels are typed functions with a dispatch table: compute/function.cc resolves an argument list to the best kernel via Function::DispatchBest, L311, compute/kernel.cc initializes per-call state in Kernel::InitAll, L62 and resolves output types in OutputType::Resolve, L447, and compute/exec.cc packages heterogeneous values into an ExecBatch::Make, L215 for iteration by ExecSpanIterator::Init, L344. This is why a filter or projection can be pushed down into the dataset scan instead of running afterwards in Python: the scanner holds an expression, and expression evaluation is just kernel dispatch.

Second, the dataset factory pattern. Discovery in discovery.cc — DatasetFactory::Inspect, L58 peeks at sources to infer a unified schema, then DatasetFactory::Finish, L68 materializes a dataset. Partitioning schemes (directory-based or Hive-style) fold into that schema, which is how pyarrow.dataset gives you partition-pruned scans of a tree of files without you writing a manifest. The writer side, dataset_writer.cc, handles the boring-but-critical constraints: max rows per file, max files open at once, and naming.

From Install to Your First Model

Arrow installs like any wheel: pip install pyarrow. The first session usually looks like this, straight from the objects we just toured:

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.dataset as ds
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

# Build a table from Python objects (table.pxi -> table.cc)
table = pa.table({"model": pa.array(["bert", "gpt2", "llama"]),
                  "params": pa.array([110, 124, 6700])})

# Stream it through IPC: writer.cc frames, reader.cc rebuilds
sink = pa.BufferOutputStream()
with pa.ipc.new_stream(sink, table.schema) as writer:
    writer.write_table(table)
buf = sink.getvalue()
rt = pa.ipc.open_stream(buf).read_all()
assert rt.equals(table)          # schema and buffers agree

# Scan a partitioned Parquet tree with pushdown (dataset layer)
dataset = ds.dataset("runs/", format="parquet",
                     partitioning="hive")
small = dataset.to_table(
    filter=ds.field("params") > 500,
    columns=["model"])

# Exit to pandas only at the boundary
df = small.to_pandas()

Three things happen under the hood worth noticing. The IPC round-trip above serializes through flatbuffers and rebuilds arrays via the loader we cited — the buffer count and sizes come back identical, because the format is deterministic. The ds.dataset(...) call goes through the factory path we quoted: inspect, infer schema, finish. And the filter compiles to an Expression that the scanner evaluates per batch with compute kernels, so partition and row-group pruning happen before your Python code sees a single row. For a training-adjacent example, Hugging Face’s datasets library is Arrow underneath — its memory-mapped shards are Arrow IPC files, which is the same machinery in different clothes.

A practical pattern for inference engineering: land your prompts, token tables, or embedding caches as partitioned Parquet, then stream them into the evaluator with dataset.to_batches(). Because batches are the native unit, you can feed a C++ or CUDA consumer directly through the C data interface without ever involving Python objects.

Where Arrow sits in the ecosystem

Arrow’s columnar layout has quietly become the interchange standard of the Python data stack. Polars executes queries on Arrow arrays natively, and DuckDB can consume them with no serialization at all — query results materialize as Arrow tables across a zero-copy bridge. The Hugging Face datasets library owes its memory-mapped multi-terabyte caching to Arrow IPC files on disk. And pandas interoperates through to_pandas() / from_pandas(), with the newer pandas Arrow-backed dtypes cutting conversion cost further. If your stack includes numpy for tensors, the clean boundary is: Arrow for columns at rest and in transit, NumPy for math inside your own code. Feather files you may have used are Arrow IPC files with a compatibility shim — ipc/feather.cc keeps the old API name but the V2 framing is the wire format we toured.

Honest Limits

Arrow is a format and a toolbox, not a database. There is no storage engine, no transactions, no index that answers point lookups quickly — a column scan means scanning the column. The compute kernel library covers relational basics (filters, projections, aggregations, joins, hash operations) but it is not a full query planner; complex analytical queries belong in DuckDB or Polars, ideally consuming Arrow arrays so nothing is copied. The dataset layer’s strength is also its ceiling: it scans files with pushdown filters, but anything requiring cross-file statistics or adaptive ordering still needs a real engine. Python’s pyarrow is Cython over C++, so the zero-copy claims are real, but the moment you call to_pylist() or to_pandas() on object-dtype columns, copies happen — check to_numpy(zero_copy_only=True) when you want the contract enforced. IPC streams are not random-access: use the file format if you need to seek. Finally, the C data interface is stable, but fast-moving corners — the dataset API is explicitly marked unstable in its docstring, and extension types have compatibility caveats across languages — deserve a test before you commit to them in production.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Apache Arrow — zero-copy arrays, IPC framing, compute kernels, dataset scanning, and the pyarrow surface, mapped end to end.

entry.title: AudioCraft Source Tour: How Meta’s MusicGen, AudioGen and EnCodec Fit Together

link.title: AudioCraft Source Tour: How Meta’s MusicGen, AudioGen and EnCodec Fit Together

entry.content:
Meta’s AudioCraft is the library behind MusicGen and AudioGen, and it is one of the most instructive generative-audio codebases you can read. It commits to one architectural idea: treat audio generation as language modeling over discrete tokens produced by a neural codec. Everything else — the conditioners, the pattern providers, the streaming machinery — exists to serve that single idea. If you have read our tours of minimal text-only stacks or high-throughput serving layers, this is what the same transformer story looks like when the vocabulary is learned codebook entries rather than BPE tokens.

The repository splits cleanly along that seam. The codec half lives in audiocraft/models/encodec.py, audiocraft/modules/seanet.py and audiocraft/quantization/, trainable on its own through the solver in audiocraft/solvers/compression.py. The generative half lives in audiocraft/models/lm.py behind the facade classes audiocraft/models/musicgen.py and audiocraft/models/audiogen.py, which share their inference skeleton in audiocraft/models/genmodel.py. Between the two, audiocraft/modules/conditioners.py turns text descriptions, melody excerpts and CLAP embeddings into tensors the transformer can consume.

This post walks that path with line-verified references from the main branch, anchored by two diagrams: an overview of the module graph and a detailed view including data IO and codec training.

AudioCraft at a glance: a thin facade (left) drives a language model over codebook streams (center), which is steered by conditioners and grounded by the EnCodec codec (right).

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything user-facing starts at the MusicGen, L40 facade, whose get_pretrained, L57 maps names like facebook/musicgen-small (300M) or facebook/musicgen-large (3.3B) to downloaded checkpoints.
  • The facade inherits the actual inference skeleton from BaseGenModel, L28, which owns both the codec and the LM and exposes generate for text and generate_continuation for audio prompts.
  • Inside the LM, LMModel, L120 wraps one embedding table and one output projection per codebook, plus a shared transformer trunk.
  • Codebooks are not modeled in parallel naively: a DelayedPatternProvider, L305 interleaves the K streams into a single flat sequence so one causal pass can predict them all.
  • On the conditioning side, T5Conditioner, L422 embeds the text prompt through a frozen T5 encoder, and melody variants reuse chroma features instead.
  • The codec core, EncodecModel, L125, runs a convolutional encoder into a residual quantizer and back out through a mirrored decoder.
  • That quantizer is ResidualVectorQuantizer, L16 — with the default bins=1024 vocabulary per stage — and it is the reason the LM problem is finite at all.

The Big Picture: Tokens All the Way Down

The cleanest way into the code is audiocraft/models/genmodel.py. BaseGenModel.__init__ takes a CompressionModel and an LMModel, puts both in eval mode, and derives max_duration from the LM’s training config. The three public entry points — generate (L151), generate_continuation (L166) and generate_unconditional (L135) — all funnel into _generate_tokens at L193.

In the simple case the whole job is one call: self.lm.generate(prompt_tokens, attributes, ...) inside an autocast context at L227–230. Tokens come back shaped [B, K, T], and generate_audio at L262 hands them straight to self.compression_model.decode(gen_tokens, None). No sampler network, no vocoder stage — the codec decoder is the vocoder.

The interesting branch is long-form generation. AudioCraft models are trained on 30-second windows, but you can ask for minutes. _generate_tokens then enters a while loop at L243 that generates a window, appends the tokens, and slides the context forward by extend_stride seconds (18 by default, per set_generation_params at L96 of musicgen.py). Each window reconditions on the tail of the previous one, so continuity is real but soft — a design we revisit in the limits section. For audio-prompt continuation, generate_continuation resamples your waveform with convert_audio (audiocraft/data/audio_utils.py, L54) and encodes it with self.compression_model.encode(prompt) at L129 — the codec path we look at next.

The Codec: EnCodec, SEANet and Residual Quantization

EncodecModel at L125 of audiocraft/models/encodec.py composes three pieces: self.encoder, self.quantizer, self.decoder. Its forward at L206 makes the flow explicit — encode, quantize, decode — and trims decoder padding. preprocess at L186 optionally renormalizes loudness, dividing the waveform by an RMS-derived scale that postprocess undoes after decoding. The public contract is encode at L223, returning (codes, scale) with codes shaped [B, K, T], and decode at L240. decode_latent at L257 stops at the continuous quantized embedding, which is what diffusion-based refinement models like MultiBandDiffusion consume.

The convolutional muscle comes from audiocraft/modules/seanet.py: SEANetEncoder at L63 progressively downsamples the waveform with strided convolutions and residual blocks, and SEANetDecoder at L156 mirrors it — the same “strided conv autoencoder” family found in most neural codecs.

The quantization stack is the part most worth stealing. ResidualVectorQuantizer at L16 of audiocraft/quantization/vq.py defaults to n_q=8 stages of bins=1024 entries with EMA decay 0.99. Residual means stage two quantizes the error left by stage one, stage three the remainder, so effective bandwidth grows with depth. The math is explicit at L80: bw_per_q = math.log2(self.bins) * frame_rate / 1000 — 10 bits per codebook per frame, expressed in kilobits per second. Underneath, audiocraft/quantization/core_vq.py holds the machinery: EuclideanCodebook at L87 maintains codebook vectors with exponential moving averages, optionally initialized by a small kmeans run at L53, and revives dead codes whose usage falls below a threshold. VectorQuantization at L222 and ResidualVectorQuantization at L351 stack that book into single- and multi-stage forms, while audiocraft/quantization/base.py defines the shared QuantizedResult container at L19 and the BaseQuantizer interface at L27.

One more codec detail matters for generation: InterleaveStereoCompressionModel at L397 of encodec.py builds stereo from mono by interleaving left/right codes into a taller codebook axis, so the same LM code handles stereo.

The Language Model: One Sequence, Many Codebooks

LMModel at L120 of audiocraft/models/lm.py is a StreamingModule holding n_q parallel ScaledEmbedding tables (L165), one StreamingTransformer trunk (L168), and n_q output projections (L174). Its forward at L221 sums the per-codebook embeddings, gets condition tensors, calls self.fuser to merge them and produce a cross-attention source, runs the transformer, then stacks per-codebook logits into [B, K, S, card] at L262.

The clever part is how K codebooks fit into one causal sequence, and the answer lives in audiocraft/modules/codebooks_patterns.py. A Pattern (L22) is a layout of (timestep, codebook) coordinates; CodebooksPatternProvider (L272) is the abstract factory. MusicGen’s default, DelayedPatternProvider at L305, shifts each codebook one step later than the previous — shown concretely in its docstring — so a single sequence step contains at most one new token per codebook and the causal LM predicts all K streams in one flat pass. ParallelPatternProvider (L359) removes the delay, UnrolledPatternProvider (L372) flattens fully, and MusicLMPattern (L530) is the flat fallback.

LMModel.generate at L421 orchestrates decoding. It asks the pattern provider for a layout over max_gen_len timesteps (L521), folds the prompt into the interleaved sequence via build_pattern_sequence (L530), then loops over sequence steps at L540. Each iteration calls _sample_next_token at L323, where classifier-free guidance happens: AudioCraft batches the conditional and unconditional passes into one forward by concatenating real conditions with nullified ones (L497–509) and splitting the logits, computing uncond + (cond - uncond) * cfg_coef at L399 — one transformer call instead of two. When two_step_cfg is set, it alternates two passes while swapping the streaming cache in and out (L381–387). Sampling then applies top-k (250 by default) or top-p at L407–416, with plain argmax at temperature zero. Note what is absent: no beam search anywhere in the decode path. After the loop, revert_pattern_sequence at L576 un-interleaves the flat sequence back into [B, K, T] codes for the codec.

The streaming machinery behind per-step caching lives in audiocraft/modules/streaming.py: StreamingModule at L20 tracks a state dict via set_streaming_state (L88) and reset_streaming (L68), and StreamingSequential at L122 propagates it through composed modules. In audiocraft/modules/transformer.py, StreamingMultiheadAttention (L138), StreamingTransformerLayer (L454) and StreamingTransformer (L577) use it for key/value caches, with optional RotaryEmbedding from audiocraft/modules/rope.py (L49) for positions.

The detailed view adds the data path, the codec training loop with its adversarial losses, and the builders/loaders pair that turns config into running models.

Conditioning: Text, Melody, and the Fuser

audiocraft/modules/conditioners.py is a 1700-line file with a simple shape. A ConditioningAttributes (L78) is a bag of named attributes — a description string, maybe a waveform, maybe a joint embedding. A ConditioningProvider (L1469) holds one BaseConditioner (L345) per attribute name and dispatches each, returning ConditionType pairs — a (tensor, mask) tuple defined at L43.

The flagship conditioner is T5Conditioner at L422, which loads any T5-family encoder — the MODELS list at L434 ranges from t5-small to google/flan-t5-xxl — through Hugging Face T5Tokenizer and T5EncoderModel.from_pretrained (L475–476), projects the output to the model dimension, and masks padding. By default the T5 weights are frozen and excluded from checkpoints (L484). Melody models add ChromaStemConditioner at L571, extracting chromagram features from source-separated stems via ChromaExtractor (audiocraft/modules/chroma.py, L16); MusicGen exposes this through generate_with_chroma at L155 of musicgen.py.

Merging conditions into the LM input is ConditionFuser’s job (L1672), with five strategies at L1687: sum, prepend, cross, ignore, input_interpolate. Text descriptions are typically prepended as extra sequence positions and fed as cross-attention sources. Training-time robustness comes from AttributeDropout (L1380) and ClassifierFreeGuidanceDropout (L1427), the latter producing the null conditions inference reuses at sampling time. The design is deliberately model-agnostic: conditioning-prefix construction in the /transformers/ sense, with audio-flavored attribute types.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is a plain pip install audiocraft (a CUDA-enabled PyTorch build helps a lot; see our notes on /torchaudio/ for the audio-side tensors). The smallest complete program is:

from audiocraft.models import MusicGen
from audiocraft.data.audio import audio_write

model = MusicGen.get_pretrained('facebook/musicgen-small')
model.set_generation_params(duration=8, top_k=250, cfg_coef=3.0)
wav = model.generate(['lo-fi hip hop with a rainy city ambience'])
audio_write('out', wav[0].cpu(), model.sample_rate)

Under the hood, get_pretrained calls load_lm_model and load_compression_model from audiocraft/models/loaders.py (L111 and L78), which hf_hub_download the config and weights and rebuild the modules through the factories in audiocraft/models/builders.py — get_compression_model (L70), get_lm_model (L136), get_conditioner_provider (L178), get_codebooks_pattern_provider (L240). audio_write (L159 of audiocraft/data/audio.py) shells out to ffmpeg for mp3/wav output, while audio_read (L116) picks soundfile or ffmpeg by format. The same pair powers continuation prompts: read any clip, pass it to generate_continuation, and the LM completes it. If your workflow involves transcription-before-generation, /whisperx/ pairs naturally here; for lightweight on-device speech, /piper/ occupies the opposite corner of audio generation.

Honest Limits

  • Long-form is stitchy. Beyond the 30-second training window, _generate_tokens re-prompts with the last extend_stride seconds of audio. Transitions are usually acceptable and occasionally audible; there is no architectural memory beyond that context.
  • Decoding is sampling, not search. There is no beam search in LMModel.generate — only top-k/top-p sampling with CFG, so you steer outputs through coefficients rather than search.
  • Sequential codebooks cost latency. The delayed pattern still emits up to K tokens per step through one transformer pass; long durations add up, and batching CFG doubles effective batch size.
  • Melody conditioning has prerequisites. ChromaStemConditioner expects stems, so quality depends on the source separation model upstream.
  • The framework footprint is real. Hydra/OmegaConf configs, xformers attention backends, and multi-GPU solver code make the training side heavier than inference; the CompressionSolver at L27 balances reconstruction and adversarial objectives — AdversarialLoss at L26 and FeatureMatchingLoss at L201 of audiocraft/adversarial/losses.py, rescaled by the Balancer at L14 of audiocraft/losses/balancer.py — and expects that infrastructure.
  • Weights are separate from code. The permissive license covers the source; check LICENSE_weights before shipping anything commercial.

For anyone who has toured text-only repos — NanoGPT, llm.c — AudioCraft is the refreshing variant where the tokenizer is a differentiable codec you can train, inspect, and reuse. Start at genmodel.py, jump to lm.py for the decode loop, and keep core_vq.py open in a second window.
entry.summary: A code-level walk through Meta's AudioCraft: the EnCodec quantizer core, the LMModel over interleaved codebooks, the T5 and chroma conditioners, and the generation loop that stitches them together.

entry.title: Demucs: An End-to-End Source Tour of Meta’s Music Source-Separation Model

link.title: Demucs: An End-to-End Source Tour of Meta’s Music Source-Separation Model

entry.content:
Music source separation is the task of taking one mixed recording and pulling it apart into its ingredients: drums, bass, the rest of the instruments, and the vocal. It sounds like an audio party trick, but it is a genuinely hard prediction problem — the model has to listen to a dense mixture and hallucinate a signal that was never isolated on the recording. Demucs, maintained by Meta’s research org on GitHub as facebookresearch/demucs, is one of the two or three models that defined this field, and it is the engine behind a large share of the “stem splitter” tools you have seen online. The current flagship checkpoint, htdemucs, is a hybrid: a convolutional U-Net over the raw waveform, a second U-Net over the spectrogram, and a transformer sitting at the bottom where the two representations exchange information. That combination is why the paper calls it the Hybrid Transformer Demucs.

What makes the repository worth a source tour is how small and legible it is. Everything that matters lives in about thirty Python files under a single demucs/ package — no service layers, no plugin registries, no tangled abstraction. You can read the whole inference path in one sitting: a CLI in separate.py, a friendly wrapper in api.py, a checkpoint resolver in pretrained.py and repo.py, the shift/split/overlap logic in apply.py, and the model itself in htdemucs.py, hdemucs.py, transformer.py, and spec.py. Training is equally compact: train.py builds a solver, and solver.py runs the epochs. The same organization also ships AudioCraft for generative audio (our sibling tour lives at /audiocraft/), so if you have read that one, the code style here — plain torch, explicit shapes, long honest docstrings — will feel familiar.

This post walks the library end to end as of the main branch (October 2026): first the architecture, then the checkpoint-to-stems inference path, then a working quickstart, and finally the limits you will hit in production. Every symbol and line number below was verified against the actual checkout, and both diagrams were generated from the real dependency structure of the code. The whole thing stands on PyTorch (/pytorch/), so tensor-level details translate directly.

The Demucs system at a glance: a thin CLI and API shell around a checkpoint registry, an inference engine that segments and blends, and the hybrid model family (waveform U-Net, hybrid convolutions, cross-domain transformer) that does the actual prediction.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • separate.main, L102 — the demucs console command: parses flags, constructs a Separator, then loops over tracks and writes one stem file per source.
  • Separator, L53 — the Python-facing class that owns the model, device, and segment settings; its separate_audio_file, L293 method is the workhorse.
  • get_model, L59 — turns a name like htdemucs into a fully loaded nn.Module by delegating to the repository layer.
  • AnyModelRepo, L148 — resolves names against the remote index packaged in the wheel, or against a local directory if you pass one.
  • BagOfModels, L29 — a weighted ensemble container; the popular htdemucs_ft variant is a bag of four fine-tuned checkpoints whose predictions are averaged.
  • apply_model, L145 — the segmentation engine: random shifts, overlapping chunks, triangular cross-fade weights, and per-source blending.
  • HTDemucs.forward, L527 — one forward pass: STFT, dual U-Net, cross-domain transformer, masking, and inverse STFT.
  • CrossTransformerEncoder, L526 — the bottleneck block where the waveform and spectrogram branches finally talk to each other.
  • AudioFile, L28 — the ffmpeg-backed reader that decodes any input format and resamples on the fly; save_audio, L236 handles the writing side.

The detailed call graph. Use it as a map while reading the sections below — the numbers in the captions match the line numbers in the current `main` branch.

What Demucs Actually Is

The library ships several model generations under one roof, and the registry treats them uniformly. Demucs itself (Demucs, L219) is the original: a purely waveform-domain U-Net with a BLSTM bottleneck, encoder blocks built from convolution, a DConv residual branch (DConv, L86), and skip connections back up the decoder. HDemucs (HDemucs, L338) added the spectrogram branch. HTDemucs (HTDemucs, L27) is the v4 model that adds the transformer and remains the default — DEFAULT_MODEL, L24 is literally the string htdemucs, and the loader prints a notice reminding you the default changed from the older MDX checkpoints.

All sources are predicted jointly: the standard four are drums, bass, other, and vocals. A forward pass returns a tensor of shape [batch, sources, channels, samples], and the loss during training is computed in the time domain, backpropagating through the masking and inverse STFT. That design choice — end-to-end differentiable decoding rather than a separate spectral loss — is what makes the hybrid branches cleanly combinable.

The Hybrid Front End: Waveform and Spectrogram

HTDemucs.forward starts by padding the mixture to the training segment length — ten seconds at 44.1 kHz by default — because convolution alignment is easier when every call sees the same geometry. Then _spec (HTDemucs._spec, L420) pads the signal by three quarters of the kernel, calls spectro, L11 (a thin wrapper over torch.stft with a Hann window), and trims the edges so the STFT output lines up sample-for-sample with the waveform branch. The FFT size is 4096 with a hop of 1024.

A detail that matters: the released model uses complex as channels (cac=True), so instead of predicting a magnitude mask and running EM refinement, _magnitude (HTDemucs._magnitude, L452) reshapes the complex spectrogram into real channels, the network predicts full complex spectra for each source, and _mask (HTDemucs._mask, L463) simply reinterprets them — the OpenUnmix Wiener path in _wiener (HTDemucs._wiener, L480) stays available for the older non-CaC configurations. The two branches then run through matched stacks of HEncLayer (HEncLayer, L69) and HDecLayer (HDecLayer, L256) blocks — each a strided convolution, a depthwise DConv residual, and a 1×1 rewrite — with the frequency branch compressing along frequency until it collapses to the time axis, while the waveform branch strides in time in parallel. A learned frequency embedding (ScaledEmbedding, L43, injected around line 360 of htdemucs.py) breaks the frequency-axis symmetry, and MultiWrap (MultiWrap, L160) lets outer layers process frequency bands with shared weights.

The Cross-Domain Transformer Bottleneck

At the bottom of both U-Nets — four downsampling stages deep, 48 base channels with a growth factor of two, so 384 channels — the model inserts the transformer. If bottom_channels is set, a pair of 1×1 convolutions first projects both branches to a common width; then crosstransformer runs t_layers = 5 layers per branch. Each layer is a CrossTransformerEncoderLayer (CrossTransformerEncoderLayer, L380) in pre-norm style with a residual LayerScale (LayerScale, L236), and the attention inside is a custom MultiheadAttention (MultiheadAttention, L725) that supports structured sparsity: the mask can be diagonal-band (diag), random, or global-token patterns, mixed freely, which is what keeps 10000-position sequences affordable.

The point of the block is the cross part: after self-attention within each branch, the spectrogram stream queries the waveform stream and vice versa, so low-level timing cues from the waveform can disambiguate spectral overlaps and vice versa. Both updated sequences are returned to the decoder, which mirrors the encoder with skip connections on each side and finally sums the two reconstructed sources in the time domain. It is a clean answer to a classic question in this literature — you rarely have to choose between time-domain and frequency-domain modeling when you can afford both.

From Checkpoint to Stems: The Inference Path

The loader is refreshingly explicit. get_model builds a RemoteRepo from a files.txt index that ships inside the package (REMOTE_ROOT, L21 points into demucs/remote), a BagOnlyRepo that parses the bag YAML files you saw above, and an AnyModelRepo that tries both; there is even a special case that detects a missing diffq dependency from the import error. Once loaded, the model is set to eval and returned.

The engine around the forward pass is where the practical quality lives. apply_model handles three orthogonal tricks. First, bags: it runs each sub-model and averages the estimates with per-source weights. Second, shifts (API default 1): the mixture is randomly shifted by up to half a second, the whole prediction is repeated, and outputs are unshifted and averaged — a cheap test-time ensemble that measurably improves SDR. Third, splitting: the track is cut into model.segment-long chunks with overlap = 0.25, each chunk is predicted independently, and a triangular weighting kernel (built around line 271 of apply.py) cross-fades the joints before a final normalization. On CPU you can pass num_workers and the chunks are submitted to a thread pool. The top-level Separator wraps all of this and handles decoding through AudioFile.read and encoding through save_audio, which supports wav, flac, and mp3 with clip-mode control.

From Install to Your First Model

Install with pip install demucs (or clone the repo and pip install -e .), and make sure ffmpeg is on your PATH — the I/O layer shells out to it for both probing and decoding. Then separate your first track:

demucs -n htdemucs "your_song.mp3"

You will find the four stems under separated/htdemucs/your_song/vocals.wav and friends. Two variations worth trying immediately: htdemucs_ft is the fine-tuned bag of four checkpoints — noticeably better on vocals, roughly four times slower because it averages four full predictions — and --two-stems=vocals writes just the vocal and a karaoke-style complement. The equivalent Python is short:

from demucs.api import Separator

sep = Separator(model="htdemucs")
origin, stems = sep.separate_audio_file("your_song.mp3")
print(stems.keys(), sep.samplerate)

If you use torchaudio (/torchaudio/), note the cross-pollination: torchaudio ships its own HDemucs implementation, and Demucs’s training script can wrap it directly via TorchHDemucsWrapper (TorchHDemucsWrapper, L36) for benchmarking against the same checkpoint metadata. Training your own variant runs through hydra configs: python -m demucs.train builds datasets (Wavset, Wavset, L107, random-crops pre-extracted wav tracks), constructs the optimizer, and hands everything to Solver.train (Solver.train, L172), whose per-epoch loop lives in _run_one_epoch (Solver._run_one_epoch, L291).

Honest Limits

Memory is the first wall. The hybrid model processes ten-second 44.1 kHz stereo segments with two parallel U-Nets plus attention at the bottom, and on consumer GPUs you will hit out-of-memory long before you expect; the segmented apply_model path exists precisely because full-track inference does not fit. CPU-only separation works but is slow — plan minutes per song, not seconds, and use --jobs to parallelize chunks. On Apple silicon the code even detours complex tensors through the CPU because MPS lacks complex support (see the explicit workaround in HTDemucs.forward), so expect the same order of slowness there.

Second, scope: Demucs is a music separator. Speech enhancement, speaker diarization, and transcription belong to other tools entirely — for transcript-oriented audio work, see our tours of /whisperx/ or /pyannote-audio/. Third, quality is checkpoint-dependent: the htdemucs name changed the default model, and the maintainers themselves note it can underperform the older MDX models on some material, which is why bag variants and the --shifts flag exist as tuning knobs rather than conveniences. Finally, training is a serious undertaking — it assumes MUSDB18-HQ, the Dora experiment runner, and multi-GPU patience. For what it is, though, the codebase is a model of restraint: a real production model you can read in an afternoon, and one of the best illustrations that hybrid architectures are not a compromise but a deliberate design.
entry.summary: How facebookresearch/demucs splits a song into stems: the hybrid transformer architecture, the separation driver, audio I/O, and the training loop.

entry.title: DuckDB: An In-Process Analytical SQL Engine, From SQL Text to Row Groups

link.title: DuckDB: An In-Process Analytical SQL Engine, From SQL Text to Row Groups

entry.content:
Most people meet DuckDB as a magic one-liner: pip install duckdb, then SQL that crunches hundreds of millions of rows inside the same Python process that would otherwise have churned through pandas loops. There is no server, no socket, no connection pool to tune. The entire analytical engine — SQL parser, planner, optimizer, execution engine, and storage manager — is linked into your process as a compact C++ library. That design choice is why DuckDB feels more like SQLite than like a warehouse, and it is also why reading its source is unusually rewarding: every stage of a query’s life is a few files away.

The repository is organized almost exactly along that life cycle. src/main owns the client-facing objects (instances, connections, result sets). src/parser turns text into a parse tree, src/planner binds names and types into a logical plan, src/optimizer rewrites that plan with roughly fifty rule passes, and src/execution lowers it to physical operators that src/parallel drives across worker threads. src/storage persists row groups into a single file with MVCC semantics. Each directory maps to a clean interface boundary, which is rare for a codebase of this age and ambition.

One structural note before we dive in: this tour anchors on the main branch as of late October 2026, and the repo layout has shifted underfoot in a way worth knowing. The classic tools/pythonpkg directory — where the duckdb.connect() Python binding lived for years — is no longer in the monorepo; the Python client now evolves in its own dedicated repository. What remains in-core is the C API surface under src/main/capi, which is precisely the layer every client binding, Python included, compiles against. So the “Python surface” in this tour is read from the bottom up: whatever your Python code calls, it lands in the same C++ entry points we will trace below.

The query life cycle across DuckDB's six subsystems: from a connection through parsing, binding, optimization, physical lowering, parallel execution, and row-group storage.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts with an instance: DuckDB::DuckDB, L404 constructs a DatabaseInstance whose Initialize, L305 installs settings, loads extensions, and prepares the buffer manager.
  • The same boot sequence calls StartScheduler, L329, spinning up the worker threads that will later execute your query work units.
  • Client code talks to a connection: Connection::Query, L97 is the thin convenience wrapper every binding ultimately funnels into.
  • The real work happens in ClientContext::Query, L904, which takes a lock and delegates to QueryInternal, L935 — the single choke point for statement execution.
  • Text becomes a parse tree in Parser::ParseQuery, L254, which hands statements to the binder.
  • Binder::Bind, L78 dispatches per statement type and produces a bound logical plan; Planner::CreatePlan, L200 owns this handoff.
  • Optimization is a separate, ordered pass list driven by Optimizer::Optimize, L539 before the physical plan generator takes over.
  • On the storage side, DataTable::Scan, L342 serves versioned row-group reads to the scan operators visible at the far right.

From Install to Your First Model

The promise of an in-process engine lands the moment you skip the ETL step. After pip install duckdb, you can query a CSV directly from disk, aggregate a pandas DataFrame in SQL, or hand results to scikit-learn without a single serialization boundary:

import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()  # in-memory database, no server anywhere
con.execute("CREATE TABLE clicks AS SELECT * FROM read_csv('events/*.csv')")
top = con.sql("""
    SELECT user_id, count(*) AS n, avg(dwell_ms) AS dwell
    FROM clicks WHERE ts > now() - INTERVAL '7' DAY
    GROUP BY user_id ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 1000
""").arrow()

That .arrow() return type is the quiet superpower for ML work: feature engineering output goes to Apache Arrow, which pandas, Polars, and most modern training stacks consume zero-copy. If your preprocessing currently lives in pandas, DuckDB can replace the hot loops while keeping the same in-memory objects — the pandas interoperability path scans NumPy-backed columns directly, and the sibling Polars engine follows the same columnar philosophy from the Rust side. For teams that build feature stages over a datasets catalog, treating SQL as the feature-definition language is often the cleanest contract between data engineering and model code.

The operational model is also SQLite-like: the database is a single file (or pure memory), connections are cheap, and PRAGMA threads=N or SET memory_limit='4GB' tune resource use per process. Nothing about the surrounding stack needs to change.

The Query Path: Bind, Optimize, Lower

The detail diagram zooms into what happens between the SQL string and the operator tree, and the code is more readable than you might expect.

Inside one query: session preparation, statement binding, the optimizer's rule passes, the physical operator tree, the event-driven scheduler, and the storage layer that feeds it.

Binding is where SQL gets real. Binder::Bind(SelectStatement &), L8 resolves each table reference into a LogicalGet, each expression into a typed tree, and each join into a logical operator with explicit column bindings. Errors you know from practice — “column X does not exist”, ambiguous references, type mismatches — are thrown here, before any optimization.

The optimizer phase is a sequence of named passes, each a small, testable rewrite. Two representative ones: FilterPushdown::Rewrite, L108 walks the tree pushing predicates toward the data sources so scans can skip row groups entirely, while StatisticsPropagator::PropagateStatistics, L66 pushes cardinality and min/max information upward so join order and aggregation strategy can be chosen with evidence rather than guesses. Because the passes run in a fixed order inside RunBuiltInOptimizers, L186, the system behaves deterministically — and EXPLAIN output maps back onto these rewrites one-to-one.

Lowering is the recursive walk driven by PhysicalPlanGenerator::CreatePlan, L75. Every logical operator gets a physical counterpart: a LogicalGet becomes a scan that emits DataChunks, a hash join becomes a build/probe pair with a shared hash table, and aggregation becomes a radix-partitioned machine that can absorb unbounded key cardinality. The generator also wires the sink/source contract that the scheduler depends on: every operator exposes either a source, a sink, or both, plus state objects created once globally and once per thread.

Prepared statements follow a shorter path on repeat runs: ClientContext::Prepare, L671 binds once and caches the plan, so the second and thousandth executions skip parsing and binding entirely. Embedded clients that want a stable ABI without C++ linkage go through the versioned C API instead — duckdb_v2_connection_create, L5 hands out a handle whose functions mirror the C++ connection almost one-to-one.

Inside the Execution Engine

DuckDB’s execution story is morsel-driven parallelism. Rather than partitioning by operator, the engine decomposes query execution into dependency-ordered work units, and worker threads cooperate on shared operator state. Executor::ScheduleEventsInternal, L83 builds that event graph: scans first, then build sides, then probes and sinks, with events rescheduling successors as they complete. Tasks are dispatched to TaskScheduler::ScheduleTask, L64, whose queues feed the worker pool started at instance boot.

Three data-structure choices make this fast. First, chunks are vectors of roughly 2048 values, so per-row virtual-call overhead is amortized: ExpressionExecutor::Execute, L86 evaluates expression trees over whole vectors, dispatching once per operation rather than once per row. Second, operator state is split into global and local halves — GetGlobalSourceState, L132 and GetLocalSourceState, L127 — so threads touch shared structures rarely and their own state constantly. Third, when work must cross threads (a hash table’s build side feeding many probes, an aggregate’s partitions being combined), it flows through a ColumnDataCollection, the chunked columnar buffer defined in src/common/types/column, which can spill to disk under memory pressure rather than fail.

The hash operators show the payoff concretely. PhysicalHashJoin::Sink, L899 has every thread append its build-side chunk in parallel before a single finalize event flips the table to probe mode, and PhysicalHashAggregate::Sink, L434 does the same for grouped aggregation with radix partitioning to bound contention. Neither operator knows how it was scheduled; the event graph decides, and the same code runs single-threaded on a laptop and wide on a 64-core machine.

Storage: Row Groups, Blocks, Checkpoints

Persistence follows the same chunk-first philosophy. Tables are sequences of row groups (large blocks of rows compressed column-wise), and DataTable::Append, L1116 adds new chunks under transactional versioning: writers allocate row versions, readers filter by snapshot, and neither blocks the other in the common case. Scans like the one feeding PhysicalTableScan::GetDataInternal, L162 iterate row groups, apply zone-map filters from metadata, and decompress only what survives.

Ingest-side table functions are the other half of the story. ReadCSVTableFunction::GetFunction, L195 registers the parallel CSV reader whose sniffer infers types, and the multi-file machinery in MultiFileReader::Create, L40 globs directories, unifies schemas, and lets one read_csv or read_parquet call range over thousands of files. Hive-style partition pruning rides on the same reader, which is why partitioned Parquet trees filter almost for free.

The on-disk format is a single file managed by the block manager: SingleFileBlockManager::WriteHeader, L1333 commits metadata updates by writing a new header with a checksummed version, so crashes leave the previous consistent state intact. Checkpointing is explicit and compaction-oriented — SingleFileCheckpointWriter::CreateCheckpoint, L235 rewrites row groups in place and clears the write-ahead log — and CHECKPOINT can be invoked manually after bulk loads to keep scans dense.

Honest Limits

The in-process design that makes DuckDB pleasant also defines its edges. One process, one writer: multiple processes cannot safely open the same database file for writes, so the “just point two services at it” deployment does not exist; if you need concurrent writers across machines, you are looking at a different class of system. RAM discipline matters too — memory_limit is a real ceiling, and while most operators spill gracefully, adversarial workloads (very high-cardinality grouped aggregates, skewed joins) can still push latency rather than throughput into the failure mode.

For the Python user there is a governance reality worth tracking: the binding lives in its own repository now, which means version skew between the core engine and the client package is possible in a way it was not when both shipped from one tree. The vectorized engine also has a learning curve at its edges — deep customization (new operator types, custom file formats) requires C++ and a rebuild, not a plugin script. And while the optimizer is excellent, it is rule-and-statistics based, not learned: pathological cardinality estimates on uncorrelated predicates remain possible, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE is still the honest arbiter.

None of these are disqualifying for the engine’s sweet spot — local analytics, feature engineering, embedded dashboards, file-format shoveling — and that sweet spot covers a surprising share of what data teams actually do. What the source tour adds is the ability to predict behavior: knowing that filters push down to row groups tells you how to order your columns; knowing that hash builds flip at a finalize event tells you why some joins stream and others materialize. The code rewards exactly this kind of reading.
entry.summary: A source tour of DuckDB's C++ core: how a SQL string becomes a bound plan, an optimized physical operator tree, and parallel columnar scans over row groups.

entry.title: Polars Under the Hood: How a Rust DataFrame Engine Rebuilt Python Data Work

link.title: Polars Under the Hood: How a Rust DataFrame Engine Rebuilt Python Data Work

entry.content:
Every Python developer eventually hits the same wall: a table too big for memory, a join that takes twenty minutes, a group-by that spills into swap. The usual answer has been to rent a bigger machine or to retreat into Spark. Polars, the most-starred DataFrame project in the Rust ecosystem, takes a different bet: rewrite the entire engine in Rust with Apache Arrow memory at the bottom, expose a thin Python surface through PyO3, and make deferred execution the default rather than an afterthought. The result is a library where import polars as pl feels like pandas but executes like a modern analytical database.

The repository layout makes the architecture claim explicit. The Python code lives under py-polars/src/polars/ — a few dozen hand-written modules that are mostly argument checking, docstrings, and delegation. Everything that touches actual bytes lives under crates/, a workspace of more than thirty Rust crates: polars-core for the columnar primitives, polars-plan for query representation and optimization, polars-expr for expression evaluation, polars-mem-engine and polars-stream for the two execution engines, polars-io for readers, and polars-python for the PyO3 bridge. The Python layer is deliberately boring; the interesting engineering is all one unsafe boundary away.

This post is a source tour of that boundary. We walk from the DataFrame a user constructs, through the lazy query stack that turns group_by(...).agg(...) into an optimized logical plan, down into the chunked Arrow columns where kernels actually run — and back up through the streaming engine that assembles results as morsel batches. Two diagrams anchor the tour; both were generated from the real repository tree on main (2.x-era, October 2026), and every symbol cited below was verified against the checked-out sources.

Polars from 10,000 feet: the Python surface defers everything into a plan, the planner optimizes it, and the engines execute against Arrow-backed columns.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • DataFrame, L207 — the eager 2-D table users touch first. Almost every method is a shim over a compiled counterpart; the class itself holds no data logic.
  • lazy, L10550 — df.lazy() converts eager work into a LazyFrame, L196, the deferred query builder that records operations instead of running them.
  • collect, L2075 — the single entry point that materializes a LazyFrame. Its signature alone tells the 2.x story: an engine parameter accepts "auto", "in-memory", "streaming", or "gpu".
  • Expr, L161 — column expressions such as pl.col("a").sum(). Built by col, L407, each call crosses into Rust immediately.
  • DslPlan, L32 — the language-agnostic query DSL. Python, R, Node, and SQL all lower into this enum, which is why the optimizer is written exactly once.
  • IR, L56 — the resolved, arena-allocated logical plan that optimize, L112 rewrites with pushdown and common-subexpression rules.
  • DataFrame (Rust), L85 — the real storage: a vector of Series, L151, each wrapping a ChunkedArray, L140 that mirrors Arrow buffers.
  • execute_graph, L285 — the streaming engine’s driver, which runs the optimized plan as an asynchronous graph of operators.

The detail view: every arrow above traces a real call path through the two codebases, from `df.group_by()` down to Arrow chunks and back.

Why a Rust Core Changes the Data Model

The single most consequential line in polars-core is the definition of a column. At Series, L151 you find pub struct Series(pub Arc<dyn SeriesTrait>) — a type-erased, reference-counted handle to a trait object. Every concrete dtype implements SeriesTrait, L212, and behind it sits ChunkedArray, L140, which stores data as a sequence of Arrow-compatible chunks rather than one contiguous array.

Two design consequences follow. First, cheap concatenation and parallel-friendly processing: appending a million rows does not copy the existing buffer, it adds a chunk, and kernels iterate chunks across threads. Second, zero-copy interop: because chunks are Arrow, handing a column to numpy, Arrow C Streams, or a training loop backed by PyTorch can be a pointer hand-off rather than a conversion. The logical type system lives in DataType, L90, an enum that spans primitives, temporals with time zones, categoricals, lists, structs, and decimal types — a reminder that a “DataFrame library” is really a small type system wearing a table costume.

The eager API keeps this machinery invisible. The GroupBy, L117 class wraps split-apply-combine, but even eager operations route through the compiled layer, so the Python interpreter rarely loops over data. That is the quiet part of Polars’ speed: it is not just SIMD kernels, it is the absence of a Python frame per row.

The Lazy Plan: Where Queries Become Graphs

The lazy surface is where Polars stops resembling pandas. LazyFrame, L196 records operations; nothing runs until collect, L2075. Inside Rust, the recorded operations form a DslPlan, L32 tree. The function to_alp_impl, L193 (“ALP” here means the arena logical plan) resolves names, expands selectors, checks schemas, and produces the compact IR, L56 representation that everything downstream consumes.

Then the optimizer goes to work. The rule driver at optimize, L112 invokes passes like PredicatePushDown, L25, which slides filters down the tree toward the scan nodes, and ProjectionPushdownVisitor, L128, which discards columns nobody will read. The payoff compounds with the IO layer: a pushed-down filter plus a projected column list lets the Parquet reader skip entire row groups using footer statistics, so a scan over a 100 GB dataset may touch a few hundred megabytes. This is the same core trick databases have used for decades, applied to a DataFrame API — and it is why the lazy API is not merely a syntax variant but the performance-critical path.

Optimization is also where the SQL story lives. The SQLContext, L229 parses SQL into the same DslPlan, so pl.sql() queries benefit from identical rewrites. One planner, three dialects.

From Install to Your First Model

Polars ships prebuilt wheels for Linux, macOS, and Windows, so installation is a single command and there is no Rust toolchain involved:

pip install polars

The canonical first query reads a dataset, filters, aggregates, and materializes — all in one deferred chain:

import polars as pl

q = (
    pl.scan_parquet("events/*.parquet")
    .filter(pl.col("ts") >= pl.datetime(2026, 1, 1))
    .group_by("user_id")
    .agg(
        pl.col("amount").sum().alias("spend"),
        pl.col("event").len().alias("hits"),
    )
    .sort("spend", descending=True)
)

df = q.collect(engine="streaming")

Note the shape of this snippet. scan_parquet — defined at scan_parquet, L520 — opens nothing eagerly; it just plants a scan node in the plan. The engine choice at collect time selects the streaming executor, which keeps memory bounded on datasets far larger than RAM. If you have been feeding model training from Hugging Face datasets, this is the same mental model: declare the transformation, let the engine decide how to stream it. Converting the result to numpy or Arrow for a training loop is one .to_numpy() or __arrow_c_stream__ call away, and for feature-table workflows that previously ran on pandas, the API mapping is close enough that most scripts translate in minutes.

The eager equivalents remain for interactive work: read_csv at read_csv, L74 and read_parquet at read_parquet, L87 return a DataFrame immediately. Under the hood they construct the same scan machinery and collect it, so even “eager” IO gets pushdown for free.

Bindings and the Two Engines

The bridge between the layers is unusually clean. Python imports polars._plr, which — per the swap logic at the bottom of _plr.py, L44 — replaces its own module entry with the compiled _polars_runtime package built from crates/polars-python. After that, plr.col(...), PyDataFrame at PyDataFrame, L20, and PyExpr at PyExpr, L44 are direct PyO3 types. The expression factory in Python literally calls wrap_expr(plr.col(name)) at col.py, L67 — there is no second expression implementation to keep in sync.

At collect time, the engine selector, L87 resolves "auto" into one of two executors. The in-memory engine implements the Executor trait, L10 with one struct per operator — GroupByExec, L23 is a good example — and materializes intermediate results as whole frames. The streaming engine instead lowers the IR through lower_ir, L235 into PhysNodeKind, L171 nodes connected as an asynchronous graph, where data moves between operators as Morsel, L83 batches — small ordered chunks that flow under backpressure, which is how the engine keeps memory flat on out-of-core workloads. Physical expressions for both engines are produced by create_physical_expr, L129, so the kernel layer is shared.

Honest Limits

Polars is not pandas, and pretending otherwise misleads teams mid-migration. The statistical and modeling ecosystem — statsmodels, seaborn, plotting conventions, thousands of small utilities — still expects pandas objects, and while interop is good, it is a conversion, not a shared object. The gpu engine option delegates to an external cudf-polars backend rather than shipping in-tree. The SQL dialect covers a large but not complete subset of what DuckDB or Postgres accept. And the 2.x-era codebase is visibly in motion: the Python package moved from python/polars to py-polars/polars to py-polars/src/polars across major versions, the streaming flag on collect was removed in favor of the engine parameter, and any source citation from an older blog post is likely stale today. The entry-point swap in _plr.py and the split runtime packages (_polars_runtime_64, _polars_runtime_32, a compat build) are recent architecture, not settled history.

There are also the inherent constraints of the design. Row-wise Python UDFs remain the escape hatch that kills performance, because every call crosses the boundary the rest of the system is built to avoid. String-heavy workloads are dramatically better than the GIL-bound era but still pay for variable-width data. And the deferred model asks something of users: code written eagerly by default will not get pushdown benefits, so the discipline of starting from scan_* matters.

None of that changes the core verdict. For tabular work — ETL, feature engineering, dataset preparation, aggregations that used to justify a Spark cluster — Polars is the fastest path between intent and result that Python currently has, and the source shows exactly why: a type-erased Arrow core, one optimizer shared by every front end, and an execution layer that treats memory as the scarcest resource in the room.
entry.summary: A source tour of pola-rs/polars: Arrow-backed chunked columns, the lazy plan optimizer, PyO3 bindings, and the morsel-driven streaming engine.

entry.title: DeepSeek-V3 Source Tour: MLA, 256-Expert MoE, and FP8 Kernels in Plain PyTorch

link.title: DeepSeek-V3 Source Tour: MLA, 256-Expert MoE, and FP8 Kernels in Plain PyTorch

entry.content:
DeepSeek-V3 is a 671-billion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts language model that activates only 37 billion of those parameters per token. Trained on 14.8 trillion tokens with an FP8 mixed-precision recipe, it reached results comparable to the strongest closed models of its generation while costing a fraction of the usual GPU budget. The architecture combines two ideas DeepSeek had refined over earlier releases: Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), which compresses keys and values into a small latent vector, and DeepSeekMoE, which pairs many fine-grained routed experts with a couple of always-on shared experts.

Most labs ship a paper, a checkpoint, and a handshake. DeepSeek did something rarer: the repository contains a compact, readable reference implementation that actually loads those 671 billion parameters and generates text with them. The inference/ folder is a handful of Python files — a model definition, a set of Triton FP8 kernels, a generation loop, and two weight-conversion scripts. It is not a serving framework; it is an executable specification of how DeepSeek-V3 fits together, closer in spirit to nanoGPT than to a production stack like vLLM.

That makes the code unusually valuable to read. Every architectural claim in the paper — the latent attention, the sigmoid routing with a per-expert bias, the 128-element FP8 tiles — is visible as a few lines of PyTorch you can trace with a debugger. This tour walks through that source with two diagrams generated from the real file tree. Every node in the diagrams links back to its file on GitHub, so you can click through while reading.

What the Repo Gives You

The checkout is tiny: inference/model.py holds the entire architecture, inference/kernel.py holds three Triton kernels for FP8 arithmetic, inference/generate.py is the entry point, and inference/convert.py plus inference/fp8_cast_bf16.py reshape Hugging Face checkpoints into the sharded format the demo expects. Four JSON configs (16B, 236B, 671B, and a V3.1 variant) feed hyperparameters into a single ModelArgs dataclass. That is the whole surface area.

One design choice stands out while reading: the code is commented like a teaching artifact. Every class carries a docstring explaining its arguments, the MoE forward pass documents its bincount-based dispatch, and the FP8 kernels walk through their pointer arithmetic line by line. For a model at the research frontier, the level of polish is more reminiscent of an educational repository than a research dump — a deliberate contrast with the weight files themselves, which are as opaque as safetensors get.

The full DeepSeek-V3 demo at a glance: the generation loop drives a stack of blocks, each combining latent attention with either a dense or an expert feed-forward, all flowing through quantization-aware linear layers and Triton FP8 kernels.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The journey starts at generate() (generate.py, L31), an interactive chat loop that forwards only the new tokens at each step and keeps everything else in KV caches.
  • Transformer (model.py, L738) is the top-level module: embedding, the layer stack, a final norm, and a parallel vocabulary head.
  • Each Block (model.py, L696) is pre-normed attention followed by pre-normed feed-forward — nothing exotic at the macro level.
  • The attention itself is MLA (model.py, L396), Multi-head Latent Attention, the component that makes KV caching for this model radically cheaper.
  • On the feed-forward side, layers one and up use MoE (model.py, L636), while layer zero uses a plain dense MLP (model.py, L500).
  • Gate (model.py, L535) scores all 256 routed experts per token and picks the top eight, with a learned bias that keeps expert usage balanced without an auxiliary loss.
  • Every projection funnels through the quantization-aware Linear (model.py, L166) layer and its dispatch function linear() (model.py, L131).
  • In FP8 mode that dispatch calls act_quant (kernel.py, L38) to quantize activations, then fp8_gemm (kernel.py, L175) for the matmul.
  • Before any of this runs, convert.py (convert.py, L33) must remap Hugging Face weight names and shard the tensors across your GPUs.

From Install to Your First Model

The demo is deliberately spartan: Linux, Python 3.10, and four pinned dependencies — torch 2.4.1, triton 3.0.0, transformers 4.46.3, and safetensors 0.4.5, all listed in inference/requirements.txt. Clone the repository, create an environment, install those four packages, and you have the code side done in minutes. The heavy part is the weights: roughly 685 GB for the FP8 checkpoint on Hugging Face, which includes the main model plus the Multi-Token Prediction modules.

Because the team trained natively in FP8, the public release contains FP8 weights only. If you want to poke at BF16 tensors instead — say, to experiment without quantization in the loop — the repo includes the conversion script for exactly that, and it is a two-flag command:

python fp8_cast_bf16.py --input-fp8-hf-path /path/to/fp8_weights --output-bf16-hf-path /path/to/bf16_weights

Next, the demo needs weights in its own sharded layout rather than the Hugging Face layout. The convert.py script performs the renames and the sharding in one pass — the mapping table at the top of the file is worth reading on its own, since it is effectively a Rosetta stone between the Hugging Face parameter names (q_a_proj, kv_b_proj, gate_proj) and the demo’s internal names (wq_a, wkv_b, w1):

python convert.py --hf-ckpt-path /path/to/DeepSeek-V3 --save-path /path/to/DeepSeek-V3-Demo --n-experts 256 --model-parallel 16

Finally, launch generation with torchrun. The README’s example spans two nodes with eight GPUs each, but a single node works too as long as the model-parallel factor you used during conversion matches your GPU count. Pass the converted checkpoint and the 671B config, and you land in an interactive prompt where every line you type is completed by the full model:

torchrun --nnodes 2 --nproc-per-node 8 --node-rank $RANK --master-addr $ADDR generate.py --ckpt-path /path/to/DeepSeek-V3-Demo --config configs/config_671B.json --interactive --temperature 0.7 --max-new-tokens 200

Tensor parallelism is not bolted on afterward — it is woven into the layer definitions themselves. ParallelEmbedding (model.py, L89) shards the vocabulary across ranks, ColumnParallelLinear (model.py, L208) splits output features, and RowParallelLinear (model.py, L237) splits input features and finishes with an all-reduce. Even the expert list is partitioned: each rank owns 256 divided by world-size experts and silently skips tokens routed elsewhere.

The Three Ideas That Make V3 Fast

The detail view expands each region into individual classes: the MLA cache variants, the Gate's grouped top-k selection, the parallel linear hierarchy, and the two Triton kernels behind every FP8 matmul.

Latent attention. Standard multi-head attention caches one key and one value per head per position, which for a 671B model with 128 heads is a staggering amount of memory. MLA instead projects each token’s KV state into a single low-rank latent vector (rank 512 in the 671B config) and caches just that plus a small rope-carrying piece. The MLA (model.py, L396) forward pass has two modes: a naive mode that materializes full keys and values, and the default absorb mode, where the up-projection weights are folded into the attention scores themselves so the cache never needs expanding. Rotary embeddings enter through precompute_freqs_cis (model.py, L297), which bakes in YaRN-style frequency interpolation for long contexts, and apply_rotary_emb (model.py, L378), which applies them as complex multiplications.

Balanced routing without a balancing loss. The Gate (model.py, L535) module is only a few dozen lines but encodes one of the paper’s headline contributions. It scores experts with a sigmoid, adds a learnable per-expert bias purely for load balancing, and — because the bias never enters the gate value — the routing objective stays untouched by the balancing pressure. Group-limited selection then picks the top groups before choosing the final eight experts. Downstream, MoE (model.py, L636) dispatches token subsets to each local Expert (model.py, L601), adds the shared experts’ output to every token unconditionally, and all-reduces across ranks.

FP8 with per-block scales. Every weight is stored as float8_e4m3fn accompanied by a scale grid covering 128-element blocks. At runtime the linear() (model.py, L131) dispatcher either dequantizes weights with weight_dequant (kernel.py, L89) and runs an ordinary BF16 matmul, or stays fully in FP8: act_quant (kernel.py, L38) quantizes the activations per 128-element tile (clamping each tile’s max and dividing by 448, the e4m3 ceiling), and fp8_gemm (kernel.py, L175) accumulates products of FP8 operands rescaled by their block scales. The GEMM kernel is autotuned over dozens of tile configurations, all in about 200 lines of Triton — a compact companion to the tensor-core tricks used by engines like TensorRT-LLM.

The same files scale across sizes, too. Alongside the 671B configuration, the configs folder ships 16B and 236B variants plus one for the V3.1 revision, and because every dimension — expert count, activated experts, MLA ranks, number of dense layers — arrives as data through ModelArgs, you can instantiate a much smaller sibling of the architecture on a single GPU and watch tensors flow through the identical code paths. The default ModelArgs in the source is itself a miniature: 27 layers, 64 routed experts, two shared experts, 16 heads. Reading the architecture at that scale before renting an eight-GPU node is time well spent.

Honest Limits

This is demonstration code, and DeepSeek says so plainly. The MoE dispatch loops over experts in a Python for loop, which is perfect for clarity and hopeless for throughput — every serious deployment instead uses a fused grouped GEMM. Sampling offers temperature only, there is no continuous batching, no speculative decoding despite the MTP modules riding along in the checkpoint, and the maximum batch size defaults to eight. The interactive prompt keeps exactly one conversation. The demo also fixes its random seed, caps CPU threads at eight, and silences printing on non-zero ranks — small touches, but each is a decision you would have to revisit in real serving.

Environment requirements are strict, too: Linux with Python 3.10, pinned one-year-old package versions, and no official Windows or macOS path. The Hugging Face Transformers library cannot load these checkpoints directly, so any experiment that starts from AutoModelForCausalLM needs a different plan. If your goal is serving the model rather than reading it, the README points to SGLang, LMDeploy, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and LightLLM as the supported engines; the reference code is for study, not for traffic. The tokenizer handling is the one place the demo leans on an external library, pulling in AutoTokenizer from Transformers for chat templating rather than shipping its own.

None of that diminishes why this code matters. Between the paper’s equations and the checkpoint’s opaque tensors sits this small, honest implementation, and it answers questions the paper leaves open: exactly where the bias enters the gate, exactly what gets cached in absorb mode, exactly how a 128-element scale tile becomes a float. Few frontier models ship with documentation this executable.

Related Tours

If you want to build intuition for the components, our earlier source tours cover the dense-model counterparts: the original Llama 2 implementation for classic multi-head attention, nanoGPT for a minimal trainable stack, and the serving-side view in vLLM and TensorRT-LLM. Reading a sparse MoE right after a dense model makes the routing machinery click in a way neither alone can. And for the training-side story — how FP8 held up over 14.8 trillion tokens, and how the auxiliary-loss-free balance was validated — the technical report linked from the repository remains the best companion to the code.
entry.summary: A guided tour of the DeepSeek-V3 reference inference code: Multi-head Latent Attention, DeepSeekMoE routing with 256 experts, and Triton FP8 kernels, mapped through two architecture diagrams.

entry.title: Kornia Source Tour: Differentiable Computer Vision Built on PyTorch Tensors

link.title: Kornia Source Tour: Differentiable Computer Vision Built on PyTorch Tensors

entry.content:
Most computer vision code you meet in production is written against OpenCV, which means NumPy arrays, BGR channel order, and operations that quietly destroy gradients. Kornia takes the opposite bet: it re-implements the classic vision toolbox — color conversions, blurs, edge detectors, camera geometry, augmentations, feature detection and matching — as pure PyTorch tensor operations that keep a computation graph. An image stops being a blob of unsigned bytes and becomes a differentiable quantity you can backpropagate through. That single design decision turns calibration, image registration, and even dataset preprocessing into optimizable, trainable components rather than frozen preprocessing steps.

The library is also one of the more pleasant Python codebases to read. Almost every public routine is a thin, batch-first tensor function: it validates input with a family of check helpers, computes something mathematically honest in a handful of lines, and returns a tensor whose shape you can predict from the signature. There is very little hidden state. Modules wrap functions, containers compose modules, and the geometry code reads like a linear algebra textbook that happens to compile.

This post is a source tour of kornia/kornia on the main branch. We mapped the repository into two architecture diagrams — one overview, one detail — and then walk each subsystem with line-linked references so you can jump straight into the code. If you want the sibling library that handles loading and model Zoo plumbing rather than the math, see our torchvision tour; kornia complements it rather than competing with it.

The overview graph: images enter as tensors on the left, flow through color and enhancement into the filter stack, while geometry and augmentation share the warping machinery, and feature matching closes the loop with homography estimation.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Ingest. image_to_tensor, L28 is the front door: it turns NumPy or PIL images into the CHW float tensors every other routine expects, and its twin tensor_to_image, L188 carries results back for display.
  • Color order. rgb_to_bgr, L29 is the small but crucial bridge to OpenCV conventions; the module form RgbToBgr, L446 lets you drop the same conversion into an nn.Sequential chain.
  • Normalization. normalize, L133 applies per-channel mean and standard deviation, and the class form Normalize, L43 promotes integer input to float first so uint8 batches do not silently truncate.
  • The convolution core. filter2d, L71 is a depthwise 2D convolution that nearly every filter builds on; gaussian_blur2d, L96 constructs its kernel analytically and runs it separably.
  • Edges. canny, L117 composes that smoothing with Sobel gradients, non-maximum suppression, and a differentiable hysteresis loop — a good example of translating a classic algorithm into tensor stages.
  • Warps. warp_perspective, L254 maps pixels through a 3x3 homography, and find_homography_dlt, L502 estimates that matrix from point correspondences by solving the DLT system with SVD.
  • Cameras. project_points, L29 applies a pinhole camera matrix to 3D points, anchoring the geometry side of the graph.
  • Augmentation and features. AugmentationSequential, L74 applies one random transform to images, masks, keypoints, and boxes at once, while SIFTDescriptor, L156 and DescriptorMatcher, L509 produce and match descriptors entirely in tensor land.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is the usual one-liner, and the first useful program is already differentiable end to end:

import torch
import kornia
import kornia.augmentation as K

# images as (B, 3, H, W) float tensors in [0, 1]
img = torch.rand(2, 3, 64, 64)

blur = kornia.filters.GaussianBlur2d((5, 5), (1.5, 1.5))
edges = kornia.filters.Canny(0.1, 0.3)
blurred = blur(img)
magnitudes, edges_map = edges(blurred)

aug = K.AugmentationSequential(
    K.RandomAffine(360, (0.1, 0.1)),
    K.ColorJiggle(0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1),
    data_keys=["input"],
)
augmented = aug(blurred)
augmented.sum().backward()  # gradients flow through blurs and warps

Three details are worth noticing. First, everything accepts a batch dimension, so the same call handles one image or one thousand. Second, the module forms (GaussianBlur2d, Canny, ColorJiggle) are honest nn.Module subclasses, so they compose with standard training loops and torch.compile. Third, the backward pass is real: kornia’s unit tests assert gradient correctness for most operators, which is exactly what you need if you want to optimize, say, a homography against a photometric loss. That property is what separates kornia from wrappers around native code, and it is why libraries like ultralytics and segmentation models such as SAM 2 can slot it into data preparation without leaving tensor land.

Inside the Detail Graph

The detail diagram expands each overview box into its concrete modules. Reading it group by group is the fastest way to build a mental index of the package.

The detail graph with seven groups: ingest and export, color and enhancement, filters, geometry and cameras, augmentation containers, feature matching, and the quality metrics that become training losses.

The color and enhancement group is deliberately boring in the best way: rgb.py alone defines the full family of channel conversions, hsv.py handles hue-space math that the augmentation stack reuses, and adjust.py collects brightness, contrast, and gamma curves. The geometry group is the mathematical heart, so it deserves its own walk.

Geometry: Warps, Cameras, and Epipolar Math

Kornia’s geometry package is where batched linear algebra pays off. The transform utilities start from constructors that produce transformation matrices directly from data: get_perspective_transform, L848 solves the closed-form 3x3 system from four point pairs, and get_rotation_matrix2d, L918 builds affine matrices from a center, angle, and scale.
