The warping functions then consume those matrices — warp_perspective, L254 for homographies and warp_affine, L385 for the affine case — both implemented by generating a sampling grid and letting PyTorch’s grid sampler do the interpolation. Because the sampling is differentiable, gradients flow back into the transformation matrix itself, which is the trick behind test-time optimization of alignments.

On top of the functions sits a stateful layer: HomographyWarper, L77 precomputes and caches its grid, which matters when you warp many frames with the same transform. The camera package mirrors this split between math and state. PinholeCamera, L36 is a batched container for intrinsics and extrinsics, and project_points, L29 performs the perspective division that maps 3D points to pixels. Depth gets equal treatment: depth_to_3d, L205 lifts a depth map into a point cloud using the camera matrix, and DepthWarper, L487 reprojects one frame into another’s view — the core operation of any planar-RL or pose estimation training loop.

The epipolar subpackage completes the two-view story. find_fundamental, L592 dispatches to the seven- and eight-point algorithms — run_8point, L512 builds the design matrix and enforces the rank-2 constraint — while the generic transform_points, L223 applies rigid transforms to point batches. Everything here is differentiable, so you can, for example, learn to weight correspondences and watch the estimated fundamental matrix improve.

Augmentation That Keeps Labels in Sync

The augmentation package is the most commonly used part of kornia, and its design centers on one problem: when you rotate an image, the boxes, masks, and keypoints must rotate with it. Individual ops like RandomAffine, L30 and ColorJiggle, L122 inherit from a shared base that standardizes parameter generation, sampling probabilities, and the return of transformation parameters. The intensity ops reuse the enhancement functions we saw earlier — the hue and saturation math flows through the same HSV conversions in color/hsv.py.

The container is where it comes together. AugmentationSequential, L74 takes data_keys describing each positional argument — input, mask, keypoints, bbox — and routes each operand through the same sampled transform with the correct resampling rules, nearest-neighbor for masks, exact coordinate math for keypoints. It builds on ImageSequentialBase, L224, which adds the plumbing for invoking children in sequence while collecting each one’s transformation matrix. Because every op reports the matrix it applied, you can invert the whole augmentation chain later — invaluable for mapping detections made on augmented images back to original coordinates. For training loops that need gradients through augmentation itself, the container is also the piece that keeps everything differentiable; the PyTorch autograd engine simply sees a long composition of tensor ops.

Features, Matching, and Losses You Can Train Against

The feature package re-creates the classic SIFT recipe as tensors. SIFTDescriptor, L156 builds gradient-histogram pooling kernels at construction time and then computes descriptors with pure tensor reshapes — no loops, no compiled extensions. Matching lives in matching.py: match_nn, L100 does plain nearest-neighbor correspondence, and DescriptorMatcher, L509 wraps mutual-NN, distance-ratio, and distance-ratio-cross checks behind one module interface. Higher up, LocalFeature, L250 bundles a detector, descriptor, and matcher into one object, LocalFeatureMatcher, L767 runs the full two-view estimation including outlier rejection, and KeyNetHardNet, L697 shows the learnable end of the spectrum — a trained keypoint detector wired to HardNet descriptors.

Finally, the quality group turns evaluation metrics into training signals. ssim, L105 computes the structural similarity index batched over images, and SSIMLoss, L91 wraps it as a loss you can minimize — the standard trick in image restoration and style transfer training. Combined with the differentiable color and filter ops, you can construct photometric objectives without ever leaving the tensor world.

Honest Limits

Kornia is not a drop-in OpenCV replacement, and the source is upfront about it in places:

  • I/O is minimal by design. The library deliberately does not read video files or camera streams; it assumes tensors already exist. The newer kornia.image container is explicitly marked experimental, and the legacy image helpers in kornia.utils now emit deprecation warnings pointing at it.
  • CPU throughput can lose to native code. For a single small image, a hand-tuned C++ implementation will often beat a chained tensor implementation; kornia’s advantage appears with batches, GPU execution, and the need for gradients, not with one-off scripting.
  • API churn is real. Feature module names have moved over the years, and the augmentation container keeps refining subtle semantics around transformation matrices and non-rigid ops. Pin your version in production.
  • Numerical parity is close but not exact. Kornia’s Canny or SIFT will not match OpenCV bit-for-bit; thresholds may need retuning when porting.
  • 3D and video coverage is thinner than 2D. Some operations exist in 3D form, but the polish and test coverage concentrate on 2D image processing.

None of these are disqualifying — they define the niche precisely. If your work lives in PyTorch and you want vision operations that respect autograd, batch dimensions, and device placement, kornia is the reference implementation to read and reuse. Start from the overview diagram, keep the detail graph beside you on your first dive into kornia/geometry, and the codebase opens up quickly.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of kornia/kornia: color conversions, differentiable filters, camera geometry, augmentation containers, and feature matching, all flowing through autograd.

entry.title: LightGBM Source Tour: The Gradient-Boosting Engine, End to End

link.title: LightGBM Source Tour: The Gradient-Boosting Engine, End to End

entry.content:
Most people meet LightGBM as three lines of scikit-learn code: import, fit, predict. Under that calm surface sits a machine written almost entirely in C++ — a binning system that compresses your features, a histogram engine that counts gradients per bin, a leaf-wise tree grower, and a set of boosting variants that share one iteration loop. The repo looks intimidating because the interesting code lives in directories with terse names like src/treelearner/ and src/boosting/, while the Python side is a thin, carefully maintained wrapper over a C ABI. This tour walks the whole stack in one pass, from engine.train() down to the split-finding inner loop, so the next time you tune num_leaves you will know exactly which code that knob reaches.

We rebuilt the architecture from the actual source (branch main) and drew two maps. The overview shows the layers: the command-line front end, the Python package, the C API bridge, the boosting engine, the tree learners, and the data layer. The detail map zooms into 34 nodes — the factories, the sampling strategies, the histogram machinery — and how one call from Python becomes one tree in the forest. Every symbol we cite below was grepped out of the tree at a specific line, so you can click straight into the code that matters.

LightGBM at a glance: Python estimators and the CLI both funnel through a stable C API into the GBDT engine, which drives leaf-wise tree learners over a binned Dataset.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Application::LoadData, L92 — the CLI front end loads parameters and data, then Application::Train, L217 starts boosting and saves the model. Its twin, Application::Predict, wires up the Predictor, L31 instead.
  • engine.train, L115 — the native Python training loop: build a Booster, then call callbacks and update() once per round.
  • LGBMModel.fit, L835 — the scikit-learn surface. It reshapes your arrays into a Dataset and, at L1128, delegates to the very same train() loop, so the two entry points share one code path.
  • LGBM_BoosterCreate, L1998 — the boundary. Everything Python or R knows about LightGBM crosses here as opaque handles and integer return codes.
  • Dataset::Construct, L330 — the data layer compresses raw features into bins, Dataset::FinishLoad, L448 materializes them, and BinMapper::FindBin, L316 chose the bin edges.
  • GBDT::Train, L246 — the engine: num_iterations rounds of gradient computation, tree growing, scoring, and evaluation.
  • SerialTreeLearner::Train, L183 — the leaf-wise grower that made LightGBM famous.
  • FeatureHistogram, L44 — the core data structure: gradient and hessian sums per feature bin, from which the best split is found.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is pip install lightgbm, which ships the compiled shared library plus python-package/lightgbm/. Your first model uses the sklearn-compatible class LGBMClassifier (declared at L1769, with LGBMRegressor at L1426). Calling .fit() does four things in order: it validates parameters, wraps your data in a Python Dataset (the class starts at basic.py L1692), sets labels with set_label, L3070, and hands everything to train(). The parameter conventions here deliberately mirror scikit-learn, so n_estimators, max_depth, and friends behave the way you expect.

The interesting part is that Dataset construction is lazy: construct() at basic.py L2499 is the moment your NumPy array is actually serialized across the C boundary, via matrix-creation functions in c_api.cpp such as the dense and CSR variants that surround LGBM_DatasetCreateFromFile, L1044. Then engine.train() at L115 builds the Booster (Python class at basic.py L3690) and enters its for i in range(...) loop at engine.py L322, calling Booster.update (L4200), which crosses into LGBM_BoosterUpdateOneIter, L2121. One Python line, one boosting iteration.

If you prefer binaries to notebooks, the CLI path is even more direct: main() at src/main.cpp L15 constructs an Application, which loads config and data, then runs the exact same GBDT::Train and saves via GBDT::SaveModelToFile. That symmetry — CLI and library sharing one engine — is a deliberate design choice that keeps the two surfaces honest with each other.

The Python Surface: Wrapper, Loop, Callbacks

The Python package is three files doing distinct jobs. basic.py is the memory layer: Dataset and Booster hold integer handles, translate between Python objects and C calls, and manage the lifetime of the native side. engine.py is the control layer: besides train() there is cross-validation via cv at L649, implemented around the CVBooster class at L367 that trains one booster per fold. sklearn.py is the adapter layer: LGBMModel at L395 implements get_params/set_params semantics, multiclass plumbing, and evaluation; subclasses override fit to add label encoding for classifiers and rankers.

Callbacks are how the loop stays extensible without touching C++. engine.train() sorts callbacks into before-iteration and after-iteration sets at engine.py L303; early stopping and record_evaluation are ordinary callables receiving a CallbackEnv each round. After training, prediction goes through Booster.predict (L4818) and persistence through Booster.save_model (L4570) and model_from_string (L4643). For a tour of how a much larger estimator surface is organized the same way, see our scikit-learn source tour.

One Iteration, End to End

GBDT::TrainOneIter at gbdt.cpp L353 is the heartbeat; everything else arranges itself around it. First, gradients: GBDT::Boosting at L229 asks the objective function for gradients and hessians via GetGradients at L242, using whatever objective was built by ObjectiveFunction::CreateObjectiveFunction, L72. For custom objectives supplied from Python, the same code accepts externally computed gradients instead.

Second, row sampling: before growing, data_sample_strategy_->Bagging(...) runs at gbdt.cpp L385. Two strategies exist: BaggingSampleStrategy at bagging.hpp L15 does classic random subsampling, while GOSSStrategy at goss.hpp L19 implements Gradient-based One-Side Sampling — keep the rows with large gradients, sample the rest. Third, the tree: tree_learner_->Train(...) is invoked at L412, returning one grown Tree. Fourth, the aftermath: the tree is shrunk by the learning rate at L422, scores are updated through UpdateScore (L502) via the ScoreUpdater at score_updater.hpp L22, and EvalAndCheckEarlyStopping at L483 consults metrics built by Metric::CreateMetric, L22. Two variants override the loop’s behavior without rewriting it: DART at dart.hpp L24 adds tree dropout, and RF at rf.hpp L26 turns the loop into a random forest. All of them are produced by one factory, Boosting::CreateBoosting, L42.

The detail map: 34 nodes from the sklearn wrapper through the C ABI, sampling strategies, the leaf-wise learner, and back out through prediction. Follow the edges from `engine.train` to `SplitInner` to trace a single round.

Inside the Leaf-Wise Split Search

Depth-wise growers expand whole levels; LightGBM instead picks, at every step, the single leaf with the best split gain anywhere in the tree. That policy lives in SerialTreeLearner::Train at L183. Setup happens in BeforeTrain at L292, which resets the HistogramPool (feature_histogram.hpp L1369) and the column sampler (col_sampler.hpp L21). The main loop at L222 runs num_leaves - 1 times: find candidate splits, ArgMax over per-leaf gains, and stop early if the best gain is non-positive — a detail that explains why LightGBM sometimes returns fewer leaves than you asked for.

The split search itself is two phases. ConstructHistograms at L412 scatters gradients into per-feature, per-bin sums by walking the binned data owned by the Dataset — the multi-value path lives in the data layer as Dataset::ConstructHistogramsMultiVal, L1305. Then FindBestSplitsFromHistograms at L481 scans each histogram, using the right sibling minus the left child to avoid double counting, and computes candidate leaf outputs through FeatureHistogram::CalculateSplittedLeafOutput — the same function that sets the root value back at L209. Winning splits are applied in SplitInner at L770, which re-partitions row indices in DataPartition (data_partition.hpp L22) and mutates the Tree class declared at include/LightGBM/tree.h L27. This histogram trick is exactly what XGBoost adopted for its own hist mode — see the XGBoost tour for the sibling implementation.

Data, Bins, and the C ABI

Everything above is affordable because of how the data layer preprocesses. Raw text goes through Parser::CreateParser at parser.cpp L261; numeric columns are sampled and compressed by BinMapper::FindBin at bin.cpp L316, a greedy algorithm that merges adjacent values until the bin count fits the budget. Bins turn feature comparisons from floating-point tests into integer array lookups, which is the entire reason histogram building is fast. Validation sets are cheap because Dataset::CreateValid at dataset.cpp L779 reuses the reference’s bin mappers rather than recomputing them.

The C API in c_api.cpp is the contract that makes the Python, R, and CLI worlds one codebase. Its shape is classic: opaque handles (DatasetHandle, BoosterHandle), an API_BEGIN/API_END macro that funnels all C++ exceptions into error strings fetched by LGBM_GetLastError, and flat functions for every operation — create, update, eval, predict, save. Inference has its own path: LGBM_BoosterPredictForMat, L2558 builds row-pair accessors and delegates to the Predictor, whose constructor at predictor.hpp L42 picks between dense-buffer and map-based dispatch, ultimately reaching GBDT::PredictRaw at gbdt_prediction.cpp L16. Serialization is symmetric text: GBDT::SaveModelToString at gbdt_model_text.cpp L315 and GBDT::LoadModelFromString at L425 define the portable format that third-party tools, including ONNX converters, consume.

Honest Limits

LightGBM’s leaf-wise growth is a trade, not a free lunch: on small datasets it overfits more readily than depth-wise alternatives, and num_leaves interacts with min_data_in_leaf in ways the docs warn about. The histogram approach is approximate by construction — bin boundaries are quantiles of a sample — so results shift slightly with max_bin and with the sampling seed used to build mappers. GOSS changes the gradient distribution on purpose, which is fine for ranking and fine for speed, but it is another stochastic knob to defend in review.

Practical limits also follow from the architecture. Training data lives in RAM; the binning pass reads the dataset once but the whole binned matrix stays resident, so datasets that exceed memory need external-memory tricks or subsampling. The native distributed backends (socket and MPI, in src/network/) are production-grade but far less commonly deployed than single-node training, and the GPU/CUDA learners sit behind compile flags, so a plain pip install gives you the CPU core only. The model text format is stable and widely supported, but LightGBM itself does not convert models — importing into runtimes like ONNX happens outside this repo. None of these are disqualifiers; they are the edges of the design, visible in the very files we toured. Between the C core and the sklearn-style wrapper there is remarkably little waste, and that is the real lesson of the codebase: a decade-old design decision — bin first, then count — still powers one of the fastest tabular learners in production today.
entry.summary: A source tour of microsoft/LightGBM: the C++ boosting core, the leaf-wise split search, and the scikit-learn compatible Python surface.

entry.title: Llama Stack Is Now OGX: A Source Tour of Meta’s Agentic API Server

link.title: Llama Stack Is Now OGX: A Source Tour of Meta’s Agentic API Server

entry.content:
If you have been following the LLM serving ecosystem for the last couple of years, you have almost certainly bumped into Llama Stack, Meta’s batteries-included attempt to standardize how applications talk to Llama models: one server, one set of provider plugins, one client SDK, and a provider routing layer that hides the difference between a model on your laptop and a model behind a hosted endpoint. In late 2026 the project took a step that surprised many people watching the repo: the README now opens with the line “Llama Stack is now OGX.” The name changed, and so did the stated mission — the codebase is no longer framed as a Llama-only stack but as a model-agnostic, multi-SDK, OpenAI-compatible agentic API server. The GitHub repository we are touring today is still meta-llama/llama-stack, the default branch is still main, and the architecture documents inside it describe the project as a server that “exposes a unified API for AI capabilities: inference, responses orchestration, vector storage, tool execution, evaluation, and more.”

Why is the source worth a tour rather than a skim of the docs? Because the interesting design decisions live in the file tree, not on the landing page. The codebase is split into two Python packages with a deliberately asymmetric relationship: ogx_api holds the API contracts — Python Protocol classes, Pydantic data types, and provider spec definitions — with no server code at all, while ogx holds the server implementation: provider resolution, routing, storage, a CLI, and every built-in provider adapter. Third-party providers are expected to depend only on the contract package. On top of that sits an OpenAI-compatible HTTP surface, an Anthropic-compatible /v1/messages dialect, and a Google GenAI-style interactions route, all served by the same FastAPI application. That is a lot of moving parts, and seeing how they connect is the fastest way to understand what the project actually promises.

In this post we walk the repository in the same spirit as our looks at Llama 2 and TGI, though this codebase is considerably broader than a single-model server. We generated two diagrams directly from the real file tree at HEAD (about 1,230 tracked files), map the major symbols with line-anchored links, trace one request end to end, and finish with an honest list of the repo’s rough edges.

The Big Picture

The overview layers of the repo: a CLI entry pair, the FastAPI server shell, the ogx_api contract package, the routing core, the provider registry, and a distribution template that turns all of it into one runnable stack.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Two CLI entry points. StackLetsGo backs the ogx go command: it probes your environment for usable providers via _autodetect_providers, writes a config, and boots the server. StackRun is the more explicit ogx run, whose run_stack_cmd validates a config file and hands off to uvicorn.
  • The FastAPI factory. create_app reads the OGX_CONFIG environment variable, resolves it to a concrete config, and builds a StackApp instance — the FastAPI subclass every request ultimately lands on.
  • A middleware stack with real opinions. AuthenticationMiddleware, RouteAuthorizationMiddleware, and TenancyMiddleware handle tokens, per-route access policies, and single versus multi-tenant mode before any handler runs.
  • Router auto-discovery. _discover_router_factories finds router factories contributed by each API implementation, and build_fastapi_router mounts exactly one FastAPI router per implemented API — which is why adding an API does not require editing the server.
  • Contracts in their own package. The Inference protocol extends InferenceProvider and declares methods like openai_chat_completion as plain Python Protocol members. Anything that satisfies the protocol can serve inference; nothing in ogx_api imports server internals.
  • HTTP routes bound to the protocol. create_router takes a concrete implementation and returns an APIRouter exposing the OpenAI-shaped endpoints, including SSE streaming.
  • One router to bind them. InferenceRouter is the server-side brain for inference: it resolves the requested model, applies access control, and delegates to whichever provider owns that model.
  • Routing tables and the registry. CommonRoutingTableImpl answers the central question “which provider handles this identifier?” through get_provider_impl, backed by the KVStore-backed DistributionRegistry. The provider lineup itself is declared in available_providers, and the starter distribution assembled by get_distribution_template picks a sensible default subset of it.

From Install to Your First Model

The quickest path from nothing to a working server is deliberately short. The README offers a one-line shell installer, or you can go straight through uv pip install ogx and then run uv run ogx go. That single command is where StackLetsGo earns its name: instead of forcing you to hand-write a provider config, it detects which inference backends are actually reachable from your machine — an Ollama daemon on localhost, an OpenAI-shaped endpoint behind an environment variable, an Anthropic key — registers the models it can see, and starts serving. If you prefer determinism, ogx run takes an explicit YAML config, and create_app is happy with either: it funnels both through resolve_config_or_distro, which accepts a path to a config file or the name of a bundled distribution such as starter.

Once the server is up on port 8321, you talk to it with a completely ordinary OpenAI client, which is the whole point of the rebrand:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8321/v1", api_key="fake")
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}],
)

Nothing in that snippet is OGX-specific — any OpenAI SDK, any agentic framework that speaks the OpenAI wire format, works unchanged. The same server also answers Anthropic-style /v1/messages calls and Google GenAI-style interactions calls, so teams with mixed client libraries can point all of them at one process. Under the hood, the exact HTTP contract for the stable and experimental APIs is written down in the repo’s own openapi.yml, which doubles as the input for generating the separately-published client SDKs.

Inside the Request Flow

The detail view: one chat completion travelling from the CLI through the server shell and the contract package, across the routing tables and registry, and out to a provider adapter, with storage and access control in supporting roles.

Let us follow POST /v1/chat/completions all the way through. The route handler produced by create_router does protocol-level validation, then dispatches to InferenceRouter.openai_chat_completion. The router first resolves params.model — a logical name like ollama/llama3.2:3b — into the provider-specific resource id. That resolution is exactly what get_provider_impl is for: it asks the registry whether this model object exists and which provider id claims it, then returns the live implementation from its in-memory map. The registry itself is a CachedDiskDistributionRegistry, a disk-persisted registry with an in-memory cache and TTL refresh, which is how multiple uvicorn workers stay coherent when one of them registers a new model.

With the provider implementation in hand, the request crosses into provider land. Remote inference providers overwhelmingly inherit OpenAIMixin, a shared adapter that owns an AsyncOpenAI client pointed at whatever base URL the provider declares, and adds opt-in behaviors like response-id rewriting, image downloading, and embedding metadata. The router resolves the model to the provider’s own identifier before the adapter is called, so adapter code never re-parses logical names — a small decision that keeps provider implementations short. Streaming responses bubble back up as SSE events through the same chain, which is why the route layer carries explicit helpers for formatting SSE error events.

The same pattern generalizes beyond chat. VectorIORouter routes vector-store operations, ToolRuntimeRouter routes tool invocations such as web search and MCP servers, and each resource family gets its own routing table — ModelsRoutingTable and VectorStoresRoutingTable are thin subclasses of the common implementation. Authorization is not bolted on afterward: the policy engine’s matches_conditions evaluates structured rules against the resource being touched, and the server’s route table maps every registered method-plus-path pair to its implementation so policies can be expressed per route.

Providers: The Pluggable Core

The provider system is the reason to study this repo even if you never run the server. Every provider is described by a declarative spec — an InlineProviderSpec for implementations that run in-process, or a RemoteProviderSpec that adapts an external service — carrying the API it implements, its provider type string like remote::ollama, its Python module, and a Pydantic config class. The registry module collects those specs, the distribution templates bundle selections of them into runnable configs, and the routing layer instantiates only what the active config names. Adding a new backend is therefore mostly writing one adapter class plus one spec, not touching the server at all.

The remote inference family shows how cheap that is. The Ollama adapter, OllamaInferenceAdapter, inherits from AnthropicMixin and OpenAIMixin because Ollama speaks both dialects — which is what makes our earlier Ollama walkthrough a five-minute setup. The vLLM adapter, VLLMInferenceAdapter, is nearly the same story for production GPU serving, and pairs naturally with our vLLM notes. Dozens of other providers — Fireworks, Groq, Bedrock, Gemini, SambaNova, Cerebras — follow the identical template.

Inline providers cover the pieces you want running next to the server rather than behind it: a FAISS-backed vector store (FaissVectorIOAdapter keeps its metadata in a SQLite-backed SQL store), local file search over those stores, and the built-in Responses implementation, BuiltinResponsesImpl, which orchestrates multi-step agentic turns — tool calls, file search, follow-up completions — server-side so a single API call can do real work. Stateful conversations get their own Conversations protocol, with the Pydantic types for the Responses API living in the contract package where SDK generators can reach them.

Honest Limits

No source tour is complete without the caveats, and this repo has some visible seams. First, the name churn is real and it leaks into the code: src/ogx/models/llama/ is today an empty package whose __init__.py contains only a copyright header. The Llama-specific inference implementations, tokenizers, and chat-format code that older material describes at llama_stack/models/llama/ are simply not there anymore — the project is explicitly model-agnostic now, and the Llama model plumbing has moved out of this tree. Anyone following two-year-old tutorials will find the paths have moved twice: first llama_stack/distribution/* to llama_stack/core/* in earlier restructurings, and now into the src/ogx and src/ogx_api packages with entirely new import roots.

Second, the client SDKs are no longer in this repository. client-sdks/ contains only the OpenAPI specification and its build tooling; the Python and TypeScript clients live in separate repositories and are generated from that spec. The tradeoff: a source dive into this repo will not show you client-side streaming internals. Third, breadth cuts both ways: the provider matrix is enormous, and coverage quality is uneven — the CI file even mentions disabling the watsonx and vertexai test lanes while their accounts are sorted out, a candid reminder that “supported provider” and “exercised provider” are not the same thing. Finally, if your need is narrow — serve one model, fast, with a tiny operational footprint — a focused server like TGI remains easier to reason about than a platform whose starter config wires up batches, files, vector stores, skills, and an admin surface you may never use.

Why This Codebase Is Worth Reading

Strip the branding away and what remains is one of the cleanest large-scale demonstrations of two ideas. The first is dependency inversion done for real: ogx_api is pure contract — Protocol classes and Pydantic types with zero server imports — so an ecosystem of third-party providers can compile against a package that will never drag FastAPI or a database into their dependency tree. The second is the registry-plus-routing-table pattern: every resource family (models, vector stores, tool groups, conversations) flows through the same get_provider_impl discipline, which is why the server can grow a new API surface without growing new routing concepts to match.

Practically, the unified-API bet has paid off well enough that Meta renamed the whole project around it: one process, OpenAI and Anthropic and Google dialects on the same port, providers swappable by config. Read the server entry point first, then one routing table, then one adapter built on OpenAIMixin — those three files contain most of the architecture. The rest is plugins, and now you know exactly where the plugin holes are drilled.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of meta-llama/llama-stack — now renamed OGX — covering the FastAPI server, unified inference APIs, provider plugins, routing tables, and the request flow from HTTP call to model.

entry.title: Inside the MCP Python SDK: Sessions, Transports, and the Machinery Under Every MCP Server

link.title: Inside the MCP Python SDK: Sessions, Transports, and the Machinery Under Every MCP Server

entry.content:
Every MCP server you have ever pointed an agent at is, underneath the marketing, a JSON-RPC peer. The Model Context Protocol defines the methods, the notification etiquette, and the capability negotiation; the Python SDK in the modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk repository is the most-deployed implementation of both halves of that conversation. When you write a twelve-line tool server or a production agent backend, this package is the machinery doing the talking. That makes it a rare artifact: a protocol reference implementation that real products are built on.

That underneath is worth a tour, because in 2026 the SDK quietly rebuilt itself. The repository now ships as a small workspace with two packages: mcp, the runtime, and mcp-types, a generated home for the Pydantic wire models that keeps protocol schemas versioned separately from session logic. The old FastMCP high-level server was renamed to MCPServer and moved to its own subpackage; the old BaseSession receive loop was replaced by a shared JSONRPCDispatcher; and a new per-request “modern” envelope arrived alongside the classic initialize handshake. If your mental model of this SDK comes from last year’s tutorials, the map has changed.

This post walks the current main branch the way a contributor would: client facades, the shared dispatcher core, the two transports, and the three-layer server stack. All symbols and line numbers below were verified against the tree at commit a525a3d9bece. The two diagrams were generated directly from the source layout, so they double as a reading order.

The SDK at a glance: client and server stacks meet in a shared dispatcher core, while the mcp-types package holds the wire models both sides speak.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Client is the front door. The Client, L268 dataclass accepts a URL string, StdioServerParameters, a raw transport, or even an in-process MCPServer instance, and builds the whole stack for you inside an async context manager.
  • stdio_client launches a subprocess. The stdio_client, L115 context manager spawns the server command described by StdioServerParameters, L94, pipes JSON-RPC over stdin and stdout, and owns a deliberately layered shutdown routine for process trees.
  • StreamableHTTPTransport carries the network half. On the client side, StreamableHTTPTransport, L111 wraps one httpx client and issues POSTs for requests while a long-lived GET streams server push; the streamable_http_client helper at L713 is the ergonomic entry point.
  • ClientSession is the typed brain. ClientSession, L388 owns the MCP layer: the initialize, L651 handshake, call_tool, L993 with output-schema validation, and callback hooks for sampling, elicitation, roots, and logging.
  • JSONRPCDispatcher correlates everything. The JSONRPCDispatcher, L264 owns the receive loop, the pending-request table, cancellation, and error responses; send_raw_request, L319 is where an outbound request gets paired with its future response.
  • SessionMessage is the envelope. Every message crossing a stream is a SessionMessage, L59: a JSON-RPC payload plus client- or server-side metadata such as request contexts.
  • ClientPeer lets servers call back. ClientPeer, L65 is the outbound surface a server session uses to ask the client’s human or model for help, including sample, L89 for LLM completions.
  • ServerSession mirrors the client. ServerSession, L35 is the per-connection server half, with capability-checked methods like create_message, L183 and elicit, L329.
  • MCPServer is the facade you actually write. MCPServer, L157 hosts the @tool, @resource, and @prompt decorators; the tool, L669 decorator is where a plain Python function becomes an MCP tool.

From Install to Your First Model

The package installs as mcp and requires Python 3.11 or newer. A server is three lines of decoration plus one line of registration; a client is one context manager away from a working call. The smallest honest example, adapted from the repository’s own docs:

from mcp.server.mcpserver import MCPServer

server = MCPServer("demo")

@server.tool()
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Add two numbers."""
    return a + b

The tool, L669 decorator does more work than it appears to. Internally it hands your function to ToolManager, L19, which calls func_metadata, L287 to build a Pydantic argument model from the type hints and emit the JSON Schema that clients will show the model. If your function annotates a Context parameter, the decorator injects it so the tool can log, report progress, or reach back into the request. On the client side, the symmetric experience is:

from mcp import Client

async with Client("http://localhost:8000/mcp") as client:
    result = await client.call_tool("add", {"a": 1, "b": 2})

That Client, L268 facade is new in this generation, and it is the piece most tutorials have not caught up with. Passing a URL string selects Streamable HTTP; passing StdioServerParameters launches the subprocess; passing an MCPServer object connects in-process, which is why the SDK’s test suite runs thousands of scenario stories without opening a single socket. Under the hood it still bottoms out in ClientSession; the facade caches resource listings, folds extensions into tool results, and only then hands you the typed calls. Tool results come back as a CallToolResult wire model — CallToolResult, L1463 — carrying both human-readable content blocks and, when the tool declares one, structured content validated against the tool’s output_schema. This is the same boundary that tool-calling models in transformers consume: the schema the SDK advertises is what the model learns to fill in.

One Dispatcher to Correlate Them All

The most interesting refactoring in the current tree is what replaced the old shared/session.py. Both ClientSession and ServerSession now ride the same JSONRPCDispatcher, L264, which owns the raw conversation: reading SessionMessage items off a stream pair, matching responses to pending request ids, applying timeouts, converting peer errors into MCPError exceptions, and running request handlers as tasks in an anyio task group. The send_raw_request, L319 method documents the contract precisely: a REQUEST_TIMEOUT error if opts["timeout"] elapses, a CONNECTION_CLOSED error if the transport dies first.

Two design details repay attention. First, the dispatcher distinguishes “inline” methods — like initialize — that are awaited inside the read loop before the next message is dequeued, versus everything else that runs as a spawned task; the docstring warns that an inline handler that awaits its peer deadlocks the parked loop, a comment written from scar tissue. Second, cancellation is policy: peer_cancel_mode decides whether a cancelled request interrupts the handler or merely marks the result abandoned, and mid-handler requests made while servicing an inbound message are routed onto that inbound request’s SSE stream via the _related_request_id channel. Above the dispatcher sit the type-specific sessions. ClientSession adds the constructor-injected callback surface — a client must answer sampling/createMessage, elicitation/create, and roots/list if the server asks — and absorbs tool listings so it can compile output-schema validators ahead of the first call_tool. ServerSession adds the mirrored server-to-client methods, all gated by check_client_capability, L137 so a server never assumes the far end can sample.

Two Transports, One Contract

The transport layer is where the protocol’s name promises live. stdio is the local case: stdio_client starts the process, deduplicates Windows command resolution, and — worth reading on its own — shuts down in ordered stages: close pipes, wait for exit, then escalate to terminating the whole process tree. The stream contract both sides honor is deliberately boring: write SessionMessage in, read SessionMessage or Exception out. That uniformity is what lets an in-process memory transport, a subprocess, and an HTTP peer be interchangeable to the dispatcher.

Streamable HTTP is the stateful network case, and the server side is the more instructive file. StreamableHTTPServerTransport, L150 is an ASGI application whose single entrypoint handle_request, L474 validates Accept headers and session ids before branching on the verb. A POST can be answered three ways: inline JSON for quick requests, an SSE stream scoped to one request id, or — for servers that support it — the standalone GET stream that carries server-initiated messages and notifications. Session state rides in the mcp-session-id header, and disconnects are survivable: if the server is constructed with an EventStore, L116, every SSE event is logged with an id and a reconnecting client presenting Last-Event-ID gets a replay of exactly what it missed. Deployment is delegated upward: the StreamableHTTPSessionManager, L45 binds the transport to a running ASGI app and keeps per-session state across requests, so a server mounted behind uvicorn scales to many concurrent sessions.

The Server Side, Three Layers Deep

Servers are stacked in three strata, and knowing which layer owns what explains most integration puzzles. The top layer is MCPServer, the decorator facade. It aggregates tools, resources, and prompts; run_stdio_async, L1074 and its HTTP sibling are the one-liners that put it on a wire. The middle layer is the low-level Server, L129: a method registry where add_request_handler, L484 maps JSON-RPC method names to typed handlers, capabilities are computed from what you registered, and a default server/discover handler exposes the modern per-request envelope to clients that probe for it. The bottom layer is per-connection state: Connection, L185 pairs a ServerSession with its request context and lifespan-scoped objects for the duration of one conversation.

The layering shows its value in the server-to-client direction. When your tool decides it needs the model — say, to summarize a 200-page PDF before extracting a table — it awaits ctx.session.create_message, which the session capability-checks, the dispatcher writes as a request, the client’s sampling_callback receives, and the client’s LLM answers. Elicitation is the same trip with a human on the other end: elicit sends a JSON-Schema form (or a URL, for out-of-band flows) and suspends until the user responds. Nothing in the high-level facade hides these round trips; the SDK just makes them one await away.

The detail map: one dispatcher core shared by both sides, transports that reduce to a SessionMessage stream contract, and a three-layer server stack ending in generated wire types.

Honest Limits

The protocol is young and the SDK says so in its own code. The version registry lists five revisions, and only 2025-11-25 and earlier are reachable through the classic initialize handshake; the newest 2026-07-28 revision — LATEST_PROTOCOL_VERSION at L50 — uses a per-request envelope that clients must actively probe for. Interoperability across that boundary is exactly the kind of thing you should test against real peers rather than assume.

Second, the renames are churn you will pay for. FastMCP still exists as a module in name only: importing it raises a ModuleNotFoundError whose message exists purely to point you at the migration guide. Tutorials, agent frameworks, and Stack Overflow answers that say from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP are all wrong on this branch. Pin mcp<2 if you need the old surface.

Third, the abstractions have seams the docstrings admit to. The dispatcher’s inline-method rule can deadlock a careless handler; the session keeps a bound-method reference on its dispatcher after exit, flagged in-source as a memory pin awaiting a rework; and stdio shutdown has four fallback stages because process trees do not die politely. None of this is hidden — it is commented — but the comfortable framing only holds until a connection hangs.

Where does this sit in the stack you already follow? On the serving side, the same tool-calling contracts are consumed by runtimes like vllm-2 when a model must choose and fill a tool; on the agent side, servers in the style of llama-stack speak MCP so clients stay transport-agnostic. The SDK’s job is to make both directions boring, and — read closely — it mostly succeeds.
entry.summary: A source tour of the official Model Context Protocol Python SDK: ClientSession, the shared JSON-RPC dispatcher, Streamable HTTP and stdio transports, and the MCPServer facade.
